Our framework predicts that the geometric strategy should be dominant when relations are familiar, whereas the algebraic should emerge to support de novo inferences drawn in context. Multiple experiments demonstrate these opposing signatures in humans, neural networks trained from scratch, and large language models (LLMs). Causal interventions in the neural networks reveal that the geometric and algebraic strategies depend on representational geometry and selective attention mechanisms, respectively, and reproduce the effects of analogous neurobiological disruptions in humans. Our framework unifies these effects with disparate phenomena, including content effects observed in human and LLM reasoning and data-distribution effects observed in machine learning. Our findings reconcile competing views of cognitive flexibility that emphasize either representational geometry or algebraic manipulation by showing that each can have unique strengths, and can characterize different aspects of both human and neural network behavior.

all_scored.title: LF-VideoQA: Evaluating Long-Video Understanding with Long-Form Theory-of-Mind Questions
all_scored.summary: The hardest part of understanding a long video is not pinpointing any one moment but synthesizing many, e.g., answering a question that requires tracking what develops across hours of content and articulating how the pieces fit together. To date, most long-video QA datasets require only a short answer or a multiple-choice selection, oversimplifying the long-video understanding task to retrieval. We introduce LF-VideoQA, a dataset for long-form, open-ended question answering over long narrative videos built on theory-of-mind questions: a character's belief depends on everything they have seen or been told, so each question demands assembling and reasoning from evidence distributed across the video. The dataset contains more than 6,300 questions on 94 recent films; each requires reasoning over scenes spanning an average of 23 minutes and comes with a question-specific rubric for recall and precision scoring. The dataset is created entirely automatically by annotating screenplays with scene events and each character's first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs, then generating (question, answer, rubric) triples through LLM-based question generation and verification; human studies validate their quality. We evaluate four families of state-of-the-art open-source VLMs across three settings and find the task highly challenging: (i) even an oracle with access to the screenplay falls well short of complete answers; (ii) the best non-oracle model attains barely half of the recall level of the oracle; (iii) unlike on prior long-video benchmarks, captions and subtitles underperform the video itself, indicating that the questions need visual evidence; and (iv) recall is the predominant bottleneck, with answers omitting many required rubric claims.

all_scored.title: On the Limits of Test-Time Compute for Self-Evaluation
all_scored.summary: Self-verification and aggregation have emerged as popular approaches for bridging the gap between pass@1 and pass@N. However, increasing the number of candidates does not consistently narrow the gap between final-answer accuracy and pass@N. To understand this limitation, we use ranking error to measure how reliably models distinguish their correct generations from incorrect ones. We show that ranking error admits a bias-variance decomposition, with both components shaped by algorithmic design choices and inference compute. Across our experiments, additional compute reduces variance, while bias initially decreases before approaching a plateau. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Scorpio, a simple and general method that jointly scores randomly grouped candidates. Across math, code, and puzzle benchmarks, Scorpio improves verification, tree search, and aggregation. For verification, Scorpio improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by up to 7 percentage points while matching or exceeding that baseline's peak accuracy with 17-42% lower inference cost. For tree search, using Scorpio to score partial solutions and select the final answer improves accuracy by up to 10 percentage points over prior methods. Finally, Scorpio improves the scaling of aggregation-based methods by 11 percentage points on coding tasks.

all_scored.title: TADA: Technology Aware DNN Accelerator Performance and Energy Estimator
all_scored.summary: Deep neural network (DNN) accelerators for edge inference must meet tight energy, latency, and area (EDP) constraints, and their optimal hardware architecture and dataflow configuration is typically identified through design space exploration (DSE). However, on-chip memory technology including cell type, bank organization, and process node, is rarely treated as a first-class citizen in DSE. For example, increasing memory capacity can reduce memory accesses through greater data reuse, but at the cost of higher area and access energy, thereby limiting the compute units budget. Consequently, memory technology can fundamentally shift the optimal accelerator architecture for a given area and EDP budget. Existing machine learning (ML)-based DSE methods require repeating simulation, data generation, and model training for each new memory technology. We present TADA, a memory technology-aware DNN accelerator performance and energy estimator that predicts system latency and energy for a given workload, hardware configuration, and memory technology. TADA is trained on a synthetic dataset that generalizes across memory technologies. The dataset spans current and future technology trends while enforcing physics-based guardrails to preserve realistic area-energy trade-offs. Each memory technology is represented by a technology signature, a vector of read energy, write energy, and storage capacity across a range of areas, provided as input alongside the workload and hardware configuration. Across 21 unseen technology curves spanning SRAM, STTRAM, ReRAM, PCM, FeFET, eDRAM, and CTT, TADA predicts system energy and latency with 1.5-4.4% and 0.7-1.2% mean absolute percentage error, respectively. In three pairwise case studies, it matches the simulator-selected memory technology at 98.7-100% of area budgets, with a mean EDP loss of at most 0.21%, while achieving over 10^4x higher evaluation throughput.

all_scored.title: Anchor 1: Precise and Stable Humanoid Control for Whole-Body Manipulation
all_scored.summary: Humanoid controllers have acquired increasingly diverse motor skills, yet translating these capabilities into precise and stable whole-body manipulation remains challenging. Manipulation tasks are sensitive to execution deviations -- even small errors or unintended steps can cause failure. Introducing Anchor 1, a whole-body controller for precise and stable whole-body manipulation, together with a benchmark spanning diverse coordination demands. Anchor 1 adopts calibrated sparse motion references to preserve task-relevant human motion structure without online joint-space retargeting, leaving kinematic freedom for precise control. To guide this freedom towards stable, physically plausible whole-body coordination, we shape the training distribution through offline curation of robot motions paired with these calibrated sparse references. We further introduce explicit error feedback decoupled from motion encoding, improving control precision while supporting flexible command interfaces. To achieve a systematic evaluation of these capabilities, a benchmark is proposed to assess precision, sustained execution stability, and reachability across diverse whole-body coordination demands. Evaluations in simulation and on hardware show stronger precision and stability across all evaluation tracks. Under the most strict real-world global scoring setting, Anchor 1 achieves a 30\% to 80\% decrease in tracking error with fewer look-ahead inputs, and without retargeting compared to all existing controllers. Downstream experiments demonstrate more efficient teleoperated data collection and higher task success using the same deployment pipeline as well. We believe Anchor 1 supports precise and stable whole-body control as a practical basis for humanoid task execution.

all_scored.title: SPARQLcirc: Probabilistic Query Evaluation with Provenance Circuits
all_scored.summary: Probabilistic query evaluation (PQE) computes the probability of every answer of a query over a tuple-independent probabilistic knowledge graph. We study exact PQE for SPARQL over graphs accessed through SPARQL 1.1 endpoints. Shared triples among the derivations of an answer make exact PQE #P-hard in general. Knowledge compilation of the Boolean provenance of every answer yields exact probabilities, and the provenance formulas of different answers can share subformulas. We propose SPARQLcirc, which rewrites a SPARQL query into CONSTRUCT queries that name every gate by its content, so that the results of independent queries form one Boolean provenance circuit for all answers. The rewriting covers joins, unions, projection, filters, OPTIONAL, difference, and transitive closures. SPARQLcirc compiles the circuit and computes the exact probability of every answer by weighted model counting. For the evaluation, we draw random probabilities for the triples of WatDiv and gMark and the statements of Wikidata and evaluate the CONSTRUCT queries on GraphDB, Fuseki, and Oxigraph. The ratio of the end-to-end time of PQE with SPARQLcirc to that of PQE by compiling the provenance expressions of the SPARQL provenance rewriting NPCS decreases with the number of derivations.

all_scored.title: Can LLM Agents Improve Imperfect Earth System Model Parameterizations?
all_scored.summary: Earth system models (ESMs) rely on parameterizations to represent unresolved processes such as convection, cloud microphysics, and turbulence. However, translating advances in physical understanding into stable, validated parameterizations and integrating them into ESMs often takes years. Agentic AI could accelerate this process and enable more systematic exploration of design choices. Using warm-rain collision-coalescence as a test case, we evaluate agents' ability to synthesize scientific literature, reimplement published bulk parameterizations, and propose new functional forms as differentiable JAX code. We compare conventional parameterizations, data-driven emulators, and agent-generated closures against high-fidelity superdroplet simulations, repeating unattended experiments across ten language models. With expert guidance or iterative feedback, agents produced executable, differentiable, mass-conserving code, although unattended performance depended strongly on the scheme and language model. Iterative feedback lowered median rollout error for eight of ten models. Retuned physical schemes matched or outperformed many learned parameterizations at substantially lower computational cost, but two of 100 unattended agent-generated closures achieved slightly lower rain-mass error than the most accurate retuned scheme on held-out simulations.

all_scored.title: Exploring Proximity and Tactile Sensing for Robotic Manipulation
all_scored.summary: Pre-touch sensing, or sensing information about an object before contact, is an attractive modality for robot hands as it can allow a robot to anticipate and respond to a contact before it happens. In this work, we introduce ToFTouch, a multimodal tactile sensor combining three multizone (4$\times$4 resolution) time-of-flight sensors with an optics-based pressure sensing array. We mount this sensor on a parallel jaw gripper and demonstrate its utility on three distinct tasks: (i) pre-grasp adjustment, (ii) item extraction from clutter, and (iii) item insertion into tight spaces. For pre-grasp adjustment, ToF feedback reduced cycle time by 7.4$\%$ by enabling anticipatory gripper closure during approach. For extraction, ToF sensing enabled successful retrieval across all tested depth offsets ($\pm$2 cm) deviating from the nominal pick point, including conditions where baseline approaches failed, with standard deviations below 0.4 cm. For insertion into dense clutter, we explore the proximity and tactile information provided from ToFTouch during an insertion trajectory. The results demonstrate the utility of multizone ToF sensing in a manipulation environment.

all_scored.title: A Hybrid Visitor Prediction Framework using Interpretable Temporal features, Integrating IQR and Anomaly Detection in Lakes in Nebraska
all_scored.summary: For effective resource management, infrastructure planning, and sustainable tourism, it is really important to predict accurate visitors. This paper estimates the daily visitation of Nebraska lakes using spatial, basic temporal, and interpretable temporal features. Moreover, we evaluate the base models with multiple metrics. Using the best three models, our method will ensemble hybrid models and choose the best hybrid technique. Further, we investigate the impact of lag features and how the models work with different outlier detection techniques such as Interquartile Range (IQR) and anomaly detection. The models are evaluated using regression metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE, and R2). Experiment results show that, after removing anomalies, MAE, MSE, RMSE, and MAPE are reduced. Adding lag features also shows some positive effects on the results. Moreover, anomaly detection techniques perform better than IQR in improving performance while preserving data. The reported anomaly-based cross-validation results favored the voting ensemble over the compared base models on the evaluated metrics. In anomaly-based cross-validation, VOTE improved prediction errors compared with MLP (256,128,64); improvements varied in the single-split comparison. Specifically, the hybrid model reduced MAE by 9.82%, MSE by 3.12%, RMSE by 1.76%, and MAPE by 6.77%. In the reported cross-validation comparison, the best anomaly-based hybrid model had lower MAE, MSE, RMSE, and MAPE than the best IQR-based hybrid model by 9.81%, 34.30%, 18.99%, and 0.66%, respectively.

all_scored.title: A Geometry-Informed Neural Operator surrogate of LISFLOOD-FP for rapid pluvial-fluvial flood forecasting: the case of Forlì, Italy
all_scored.summary: Physically based two-dimensional hydraulic models are too slow for real-time inundation forecasting and large ensembles. We present a time-dependent geometry-informed neural operator (GINO) surrogate of LISFLOOD-FP for the municipality of Forlì (Italy), severely affected by the May 2023 Emilia-Romagna floods. The surrogate is designed for an operational setting in which only river stage gauges and rain gauges are available. A reproducible pipeline turns public regional observations into a physically based training set: each river inflow is driven by the first stage gauge downstream of it through a calibrated water-surface boundary condition, and rain enters as SCS-CN effective rainfall. The surrogate is an autoregressive GINO trained on 216 simulations of 24 observed events with scaled forcing. It predicts volume-conserving polygon-mean depths on an exposure-based Voronoi mesh of 659 nodes, with a 20 min step over 72 h. The surrogate is tested on 38 independent observed events that it never saw during training. On these events it reaches a critical success index (CSI) of 0.934 at 0.05m and 0.844 at 0.3 m, a depth RMSE of 0.008m and an $R^2$ of 0.984 for maximum-depth maps. On one NVIDIA A10G GPU a 72-h forecast takes 1.7 s instead of 55 s with LISFLOOD-FP, and a 50-member ensemble, computed in a single batched rollout, takes 6.2 s instead of about 46 min, which makes probabilistic flood forecasting practical. These results show that neural-operator surrogates can deliver accurate pluvial-fluvial flood forecasts driven by river stage for operational early warning.

all_scored.title: VerifLM: Physically Verified Image-Edit-Guided Goal Pose Generation for Robotic Manipulation
all_scored.summary: Many manipulation goals are easier to visualize than to specify numerically through explicit geometric constraints. We present VerifLM, a framework that converts image-edited goal configurations into physically verified 6-DoF object poses for planning. Using an edited image, VerifLM recovers an initial relative pose between an active object and a passive object, then prompts a vision-language model to generate axis-wise sampling constraints and a task-specific validation program. Candidate poses are evaluated in a physics simulator, and the VLM selects the most task-consistent retained candidate. To operate without predefined object meshes or physical parameters, VerifLM reconstructs metric object geometry from RGB-D observations and constructs multiple hypothetical simulations with varying physics and geometry. Parallel-world validation evaluates candidates across geometry--physics variations and ranks them by the number of worlds in which they satisfy the validation program. We evaluate VerifLM on nine manipulation tasks. VerifLM achieves the highest task success on eight of nine tasks, with the largest performance gain on goals requiring precise orientation and contact relationships.

all_scored.title: MoSoLoco: Monocular 3D Human Localization through Visual Latent Features and Social Context
all_scored.summary: Estimating the metric 3D position of people from a monocular camera is important for robot navigation and motion prediction. Lightweight pose-based localizers are attractive for robotic hardware with limited computational resources because they operate on compact 2D keypoints. However, they typically discard the richer visual representations computed by the pose estimator. We introduce MoSoLoco, a per-frame monocular 3D human localizer that combines the pose detector's internal visual features with the detected 2D skeleton, without requiring an additional RGB or depth encoder. MoSoLoco can further incorporate sparse same-frame multi-person context to refine individual position estimates. Experiments on JRDB and NuScenes show that reusing pose-detector representations improves localization, reducing the best JRDB error by approximately 23 percent relative to the strongest evaluated keypoint-based baseline. A sparse social-interaction module incorporates nearby detections from the same image for further refinement. Controlled trajectory-forecasting experiments show downstream benefits, while the complete pipeline remains suitable for efficient Jetson AGX Xavier inference.

all_scored.title: CUA-Master: Scaling Computer-use Agents through Open-World Recursive Improvements
all_scored.summary: Despite recent advances in CUAs, their development remains constrained by the limited diversity, controllability, and reliability of interaction data. Moreover, conventional optimization pipelines lack iterative feedback, while existing recursive improvement approaches often rely on self-generated experiences, limiting ability expansion and yielding diminishing returns. To address these challenges, we introduce CUA-Master, a nested double-loop recursive improvement framework. At the system level, an outer world-data-model flywheel continuously incorporates open-world corpus and leverages evolving model weaknesses to guide subsequent data construction and optimization iterations. At the data level, an inner flywheel couples open-world seeding and autocatalytic propagation. The former mines authentic workflows as seed tasks from instructional videos, and employs visual-semantic dual-path trajectory reconstruction; The latter transforms these seeds into reusable primitives for controllable synthesis of diverse, complex, and verifiable tasks. To enable efficient and reliable trajectory collection, we further introduce a feedback-guided snapshot-rollback retry mechanism in various real environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUA-Master-27B achieves competitive performance across GUI-only and GUI-CLI hybrid benchmarks, scoring 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0, 43.9 on WeaveBench, and 25.0 on Agents' Last Exam. Our framework also substantially improves the quality and efficiency of data synthesis, and exhibits continuous gains across recursive iterations.

all_scored.title: Multimodal Prompt Learning with Dual-Granularity Contrastive Alignment for Preoperative Prediction of Lung Adenocarcinoma Invasiveness Using 3D CT
all_scored.summary: Accurate preoperative prediction of lung adenocarcinoma invasiveness is important for surgical planning and individualized treatment. However, overlapping CT appearances make it challenging to distinguish invasive adenocarcinoma (IAD) from Pre-IAD lesions. We propose a multimodal prompt-learning framework with dual-granularity image-text alignment for 3D CT-based IAD classification. A 3D ResNet-CBAM encoder extracts global and spatial visual features. A frozen RadBERT backbone is adapted with separate learnable prompts for report-level and keyword-level text encoding. These prompts are initialized using semantic representations derived from real-world clinical reports. Global contrastive alignment connects whole-volume CT representations with reports generated from clinician-annotated radiological attributes to provide overall semantic supervision. A multiple instance learning-based local alignment module associates spatial CT features with vascular-focused radiological keywords, to capture local imaging characteristics potentially associated with tumor invasion. The framework jointly optimizes classification and alignment objectives, while inference requires only CT images. Experiments included 1,593 pathologically confirmed nodules. On the test set, the proposed method achieved an accuracy of 87.92%, F1-score of 87.78%, and AUC of 0.9499. Its AUC significantly exceeded that of the image-only Res-CBAM baseline with the same visual backbone (0.9297; DeLong test, p = 0.0078). Ablation analyses supported the complementary contributions of global and local alignment and the benefit of report-based prompt initialization. Qualitative visualizations showed activation within nodules and adjacent vascular structures. These findings suggest that dual-granularity radiological supervision can enhance CT-based invasiveness prediction while preserving a CT-only inference workflow.

all_scored.title: Comparative study of global pooling for pre-departure ship fuel consumption prediction: Advantages over per-ship and adaptation-based approaches
all_scored.summary: Most fuel oil consumption (FOC) models for voyage planning are per-ship models and thus generalize poorly beyond each vessel's records. Transfer and federated learning have been reported to perform better, but under different protocols that often use inputs unavailable before departure or random data splits. It therefore remains unclear which approach performs best. In this study, we compare 11 per-ship, adaptation-based, and global methods on 21 vessels. To prevent leakage, all methods receive identical inputs known or forecast before departure, excluding engine RPM and shaft power, and are tested on intact voyage legs after all training records of each vessel. Global pooling, in which one model describes each vessel by its ship identity and seven ship specifications, performs best overall in every setting examined. For in-fleet vessels, Global LightGBM reaches an overall MAPE of 8.92%, against 11.14% for Per-Ship LightGBM, and outperforms every per-ship and adaptation-based model. Global models of five architectures, including a Transformer, all outperform the per-ship and federated models. Fine-tuning a global model for each vessel, even by low-rank adaptation of the Transformer, adds no accuracy. Without any records of a vessel, the global model reaches a median MAPE of 11.20% and outperforms a per-ship model trained on that vessel's records for 14 of 21 vessels. Adding its first records to the pooled data is as accurate as vessel-specific adaptation. Ship identity and specifications are largely interchangeable for in-fleet vessels, but only the specifications support zero-shot prediction. Its error grows as a vessel's specifications differ from the fleet's. Per-ship models and vessel-specific adaptation are therefore unnecessary under fair comparison. One global model can serve a whole fleet, including newly delivered vessels with similar specifications.

all_scored.title: SyncHeC: Markerless Spatio-Temporal Hand-Eye Calibration via Differentiable Rendering and Continuous-Time Joint Optimization
all_scored.summary: Markerless hand-eye calibration under continuous motion requires jointly resolving camera geometry and the time offset between images and joint states. We present SyncHeC (Synchronized Hand-Eye Calibration), a dense differentiable-rendering framework that estimates both from a single robot trajectory. Continuous-time forward kinematics makes latency differentiable, metric depth complements mask contours, and an offline planner combines spatial sensitivity with temporal excitation. Alternating updates support Eye-to-Hand, Eye-in-Hand, and multi-camera calibration. On a 7-DoF arm, one $6.5$\,s motion yields $0.21$\,cm translation error against a marker-board reference, $0.34$\,cm touch-test error, and $2.7$\,ms latency error relative to an $87$\,ms reference with $95\%$ uncertainty of $\pm1.5$\,ms. Against CM-Calib on matched recordings, translation and nominal latency errors improve by $3.7\times$ and $2.3\times$. Experiments span seven arms and four depth sensors. Compensating the recovered offset during policy training and deployment increases success by $8.1$ percentage points across six families and six tasks ($1{,}800$ matched pairs; paired $95\%$ confidence interval $[6.3,9.9]$ points).

all_scored.title: ReContact: Reconstruct and Retarget Human Contacts from Video for Contact-Rich Humanoid Manipulation
all_scored.summary: Contact transitions allow humanoid robots to redistribute object support across the whole body, enabling manipulation beyond hand-only grasps. Human videos provide a scalable source of such transitions for robots to learn from. However, body occlusion disrupts object pose tracking and corrupts retargeted motion. Moreover, accurately reproducing the object trajectory does not ensure that the robot applies stabilizing forces at the intended contacts, risking slips or drops in later phases. To address these challenges, we propose ReContact, which reconstructs and retargets human-object interactions through an object-centric contact plan. The plan specifies contact phases, contact pairs, anchors, pressing directions, and sticking or sliding modes. Contact priors stabilize object pose reconstruction through occlusion. A residual policy over a frozen whole-body tracker is rewarded for making contact at planned anchors with forces aligned to the specified directions. In simulation, on a thigh-supported regrasp task, ReContact achieves the planned two-palm bottom hold in 83.5 of episodes over three training seeds, versus 0.16% for the best adapted baseline. One policy trained on 247 references re-solved for new placements raises in-workspace tube-transfer success from 20.4% (source reference only) to 97.8%. On a real Unitree G1, policies execute seven contact-rich manipulation and two loco-manipulation tasks.

all_scored.title: Generative diffusion in long-range correlated landscapes: Speciation cascade and the foam structure of the score
all_scored.summary: While state of the art for image and video generation, the fundamental reasons for the effectiveness of generative diffusion remain unclear. In particular, the observed advantage of following an entire reverse process with respect to single-shot or autoregressive methods, and for what type of data it may hold, is not well understood. In this work, we aim to better understand the role of the reverse process by considering a complex yet analytically tractable data model, the Gibbs measure of a high-dimensional Gaussian random potential with long-range correlations. Focusing on the exact score, we show that the speciation threshold, in which a trajectory commits to one class of the data, becomes a speciation window, in which the reverse process progressively resolves the Parisi tree of pure states of the full replica-symmetry breaking measure, committing to ever finer branches down to a single pure state. Importantly, these commitments take place at noise levels where the noisy sample distinguishes the pure states only through an energy of order one, beyond the reach of standard replica saddle points. Constructing a Larkin argument suited to such $O(1)$ energy gaps, we describe the score as a foam, with slab-like cells separated by shock-like boundaries. In the variance-exploding process we consider, this window is followed by a shrinkage of the samples towards the data support, and finally by reconstruction within the selected pure state. The denoising error of the exact score follows these stages, dropping during the speciation window with a profile set by the Parisi function alone, and then within the selected state. We believe that the generative foam we describe, and in particular the boundaries between cells, could play an important role in determining where the errors of trained diffusion models redistribute the mass of the generated samples when the data are long-range correlated.

all_scored.title: PointPilot: Unified Robotic Manipulation via Object-Centric 3D Point Flow Prediction
all_scored.summary: Generalization remains a central challenge in robotics, calling for policies that address domain variations from multiple dimensions such as diverse embodiments, camera poses, and/or scene layouts. In order to approach this problem, we introduce PointPilot, a task-focused and 3D aligned manipulation framework built on a 3D space point-flow prediction. Rather than modeling the global scene, PointPilot only represents task-focused objects (robot grippers treated as objects), avoiding the prediction of potentially redundant scene parts unrelated to the manipulation tasks. Moreover, PointPilot aligns 3D spatial representation in one unified coordinate and supports closed-loop and fully automatic action execution across different manipulation modes from object point flow without a separately trained action expert, while existing works typically need an extra action head or are (semi-)automatic and single-arm mode specific. Given sensor observations and language instructions, our model jointly learns subtask planning, task-relevant object grounding, and 3D point flow prediction in an end-to-end way. By processing heterogeneous data in a shared 3D point flow space, PointPilot is able to absorb demonstrations from different embodiments. Extensive simulative and real world experiments validate our method. Notably, we demonstrate zero-shot embodiment generalization with PointPilot. A single trained policy can be deployed on previously unseen embodiments and successfully complete manipulation tasks without any additional fine-tuning.

all_scored.title: JABER: Sequential Quality Control for Human-AI Data Annotation under Shared Bias
all_scored.summary: High-quality annotations are essential for training and evaluating artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Quality control (QC) often acquires additional human or AI judgments before accepting a label. Nevertheless, shared biases can cause correlated judgments, leading conventional methods to mistake repeated agreement for independent evidence of correctness. To address this challenge, we propose JABER (Joint Alias-Preserving Belief for Evidence Routing), a bias-aware sequential QC framework that maintains a joint Bayesian posterior over label correctness and shared biases to guide evidence acquisition and termination decisions. Building on this posterior, we develop a finite-horizon algorithm that selects evidence-acquisition and termination actions to minimize expected QC loss under resource constraints. Our theoretical analysis shows that conditional-independence updating can become arbitrarily confident in an incorrect label under persistent shared bias. We further identify when repeated inspections cannot distinguish a correct label from an incorrect label supported by shared bias, when obtaining a new label can resolve this ambiguity, and why modeling the dependence between label correctness and shared bias can be necessary for QC decisions. Our experiments show that JABER reduces expected QC loss by an average of 4.65% compared with a method maintaining separate label correctness and bias probabilities when shared bias makes repeated inspections unreliable. Further, JABER's finite-horizon planning, which evaluates outcomes of successive QC actions, reduces expected QC loss by an average of 10.05% compared with a one-step lookahead method. In real-API experiments on FEVER, JABER achieves zero labeling errors while reducing QC costs by 2.67% and 16.99% compared with marginal-based belief modeling and one-step lookahead methods, respectively.

all_scored.title: Gibbs Variational Last Layers for Long-Horizon Dynamics Learning
all_scored.summary: Accurate long-horizon probabilistic predictions of dynamical systems are a prerequisite for model-based decision-making. Variational Bayesian last layers (VBLLs) are an attractive model class for this setting, offering tractable uncertainty at near-deterministic cost, yet they are trained exclusively with single-step likelihood objectives that may be insufficient for reliable multi-step rollouts. We revisit VBLLs through the lens of Gibbs variational inference, which decouples posterior inference from the choice of training loss. Building on this perspective, we introduce a family of multi-step training losses that progressively incorporate long-horizon structure, robustness via continuous ranked probability scores (CRPS), and training on full autoregressive rollouts. Our approach retains the simplicity of VBLLs while directly optimizing for multi-step predictive quality. Across illustrative synthetic environments, a diverse suite of chaotic dynamical systems, and real-world data, we show that multi-step, CRPS-based objectives substantially improve long-horizon accuracy and distributional fit, consistently outperforming single-step likelihood training.

all_scored.title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding
all_scored.summary: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by reducing the sequential cost of token-by-token generation. Advanced SD methods reduce proposal cost with parallel drafters that predict entire blocks in one forward pass, but overall speedup still depends on acceptance length. On-policy distillation (OPD) can push well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus, yet conventional pipelines collect supervision through sequential draft-and-verify rollouts. Our key insight is that on-policy supervision need not inherit these dependencies: a draft block can be supervised using only its reference prefix and draft-sampled history. We propose SpecOPD, a branch-parallel OPD framework that parallelizes draft sampling and target supervision across independent branches drawn from the evolving drafter policy at reference anchors. We pack these branches into proposal trees to share target-prefix computation, using tree masks for full attention, branch-consistent indexer groups for sparse attention, and indexed state replay for linear attention to preserve each branch's history. We train the drafter with an E2E-TV surrogate that directly targets acceptance length. Our study spans 8B full-attention (GQA), 27B full-linear (GQA--GDN), and 125B sparse-linear (QSA--GDN) targets, three parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2), and four task domains (dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic). SpecOPD achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, $16.09\times$ supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD under native configurations, and up to $3.56\times$ generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.

all_scored.title: CARE: Contrastive Representation Learning with Environment-Invariance Regularization for Behavioural Intention Prediction
all_scored.summary: Trajectory-based behavioural intention prediction faces environmental variation, and representations learned with a pooled contrastive objective may retain environment-specific regularities. We present CARE, a self-supervised trajectory-learning framework that couples temporally asymmetric contrastive views with an invariant-risk-minimisation (IRM)-style gradient penalty on environment-wise contrastive risks. Each input window yields an anchor, a partially masked positive view, and a temporally perturbed negative view. Masked reconstruction and observability-aware evidence consistency complement this objective by promoting temporal information retention under partial input. On an IMPTC-derived four-class intention task, CARE achieves 0.840 accuracy and 0.023 expected calibration error (ECE) under IID fine-tuning, and 0.806 accuracy with a Brier score of 0.308 on the reported held-out environment. Under frozen-encoder linear probing, reconstruction provides the largest individual held-out accuracy gain, whereas the complete objective yields the lowest held-out ECE (0.049) among tested variants. These results support the combined objective as a competitive representation-learning approach under the evaluated shift, while the IRM-style regulariser is not taken as evidence of formal invariance.

all_scored.title: The Staged Pandora's Box: Reservation Indices for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
all_scored.summary: A staged search must decide which candidate to advance next and when to stop. Some observations only inform later decisions; others can be kept as results. We formulate these choices as a staged Pandora's box with a designated set of collectable stages. For independent finite-stage candidates with bounded readings and positive bounded own-history costs, an exact covered-call recursion gives the reservation index, the optimal value and the loss of every advance or stop; advancing an index-maximal candidate while its index exceeds the incumbent is optimal. The representation recovers classical single-stage search, nested inspection and the all-collectable Markov setting, and prices changes in the problem: enlarging the collectable set or lowering costs raises the value by an explicit covered-call overshoot. Resumption can be valuable even when future reward laws do not change, but has no value for deterministic readings. With information sharing across candidates, no rule using only their separate remaining-reading laws is universally optimal, and making an intermediate reading collectable can change which candidate is inspected first. Under a coherent joint path law with own-history costs, an approximate-planning bound controls the recomputed index's regret by changes in untouched candidates' local values; a common-component specialization bounds those changes through predictive total-variation dispersion. Exact finite-law experiments check the representation, the loss accounting and the bounds.

all_scored.title: Visuo-tactile Diffusion Policy for Robotic Manipulation with Auxiliary Tactile Dynamics Prediction
all_scored.summary: Long-horizon robotic assembly requires reliable perception and action across grasping, alignment, and insertion. Vision captures global object pose and scene context, where as fingertip touch provides local contact cues that are especially useful as contact states change. We present a visuotactile diffusion policy that combines four-step histories from two camera views and two fingertip tactile images to condition action-sequence generation. A recurrent temporal representation integrates recent observations from both modalities. To encourage it to capture how contact evolves under action, an auxiliary objective predicts fingertip-image changes two steps ahead from the temporal representation and demonstrated actions. This objective is used only during training and adds no inference-time computation. Across three independent training seeds in MuJoCo assembly experiments, the full model achieves an average success rate of $59.0\% \pm 2.6\%$, improving on the visual-only baseline ($42.7\% \pm 1.5\%$) by 16.3 percentage points.

all_scored.title: Energy-Based Policy Orchestration
all_scored.summary: Hierarchical control scales robot behavior by separating task-level planning from low-level control. In dynamic, high-dimensional tasks, however, a fixed planner-to-policy interface can fail when contacts, balance, or disturbances evolve faster than high-level policy updates. Execution therefore requires choosing not only which low-level policy to run, but also which policy-specific goal should be given to it. We formulate this problem as policy orchestration: runtime selection of a policy-goal pair that is likely to remain feasible while tracking the planner target. We develop EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator for modular goal-conditioned policy families. For each policy, EPO learns a composite energy over low-level goals, where lower energy corresponds to higher feasibility and more accurate target realization. At runtime, EPO refines each policy's goal and executes the lowest-energy policy-goal pair. Because energies are policy-specific, new policies can be incorporated by learning their own energy models, without retraining the existing policies or a centralized scheduler. In simulation, EPO improves the empirical precision-robustness trade-off by refining policy-specific goals before selectively switching among policies based on energy scores. We further demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of the same frozen policies and energy models on real humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://yewr.github.io/epo

all_scored.title: End-to-End Stability of Online Active Learning in Large-Scale Neural Systems
all_scored.summary: Online Active Learning (OAL) aims to extend deep learning from static inference after offline training to continuous adaptation during real-time interaction with a changing physical environment. This transition is essential for safety-critical applications, but it raises a central theoretical question: whether the online parameter update process remains stable when scaled to multilayer neural architectures. This paper develops a stability-focused OAL framework. The framework uses prediction error as a feedback signal to update a structured deep model, thereby linking online learning with Lyapunov-based energy minimization. We show that prediction error convergence alone is insufficient for global parameter convergence because multilayer networks may admit high-dimensional manifolds of equivalent output solutions. The analysis therefore separates output error regulation, internal zero dynamics, interlayer coupling, and parameter convergence. Persistency of excitation and active damping are then used to remove the residual null-space modes that remain after output error convergence. A cascaded Lyapunov analysis establishes asymptotic stability of the overall OAL learning process, while monotonic activation functions and diffeomorphic layer mappings provide the uniqueness condition for the target parameter trajectory. The resulting proof provides a theoretical basis for applying online adaptive learning to large-scale neural systems in nonstationary and safety-critical settings.

all_scored.title: When Does Adaptive Halting Win? Selection Rules Matter in Looped Language Models
all_scored.summary: Looped language models can stop iterating early, and recent work shows that post-hoc readouts of the loop trajectory often rival the learned exit gate of the looped model Ouro. Such comparisons reduce each method to one operating point chosen by a selection rule. We ask whether that rule decides the outcome. On a frozen Ouro-1.4B with four loops, we compared a trained stability probe ($π_1$-x) with Ouro's native gate, adapted to a per-question stopping decision, in pre-registered studies; the confirmatory study was designed after an exploratory finding on development data and evaluated once on a sealed test set of 8,517 questions. In the pre-registered confirmatory comparison, which selected operating points with a bootstrap-screened 1 pp accuracy-loss rule, the probe saved more of the four-loop budget than the native gate (+0.053 gross macro saving over three benchmarks, 95% CI [+0.049, +0.057]), mostly from CommonsenseQA, where the probe's test upper bound on accuracy loss exceeded 1 pp. Under a point-only rule, a pre-specified secondary analysis on the same test set reversed the preference (-0.022 [-0.026, -0.018]), with operating points that exceeded the budget. In pre-specified secondary comparisons, the probe showed no demonstrated advantage over an untrained KL divergence between successive loops (+0.00125 [-0.0041, +0.0065]); we emphasise this result post hoc and claim no equivalence. The probe also broke its budget on one of two out-of-distribution benchmarks (3.26 pp loss on Social IQa). Savings are estimated from stored full-depth traces, not measured inference time, and our screen carries no formal risk-control guarantee. We conclude that halting methods should be compared as signals together with selection procedures, with strong untrained baselines and out-of-distribution checks.

all_scored.title: Toward Agentic AI-Ready Workflows in Built Environment Organizations: Knowledge Structures and Interoperability Challenges
all_scored.summary: The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in the built environment is shifting attention from isolated AI tools toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act across project and organizational workflows. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on large language model capabilities, but also on the readiness of heterogeneous data environments across the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector. These environments combine structured sources, such as CAD and BIM models, schedules, cost databases, and asset registers, with unstructured ones, including technical reports, design narratives, planning and policy documents, contracts, meeting minutes, and risk registers. This paper reviews how built environment data can be organized to support agentic AI-ready workflows, focusing on knowledge structures, interoperability, and access and integration mechanisms such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Drawing on existing literature, it examines approaches proposed to organize structured and unstructured data and considers how such data can be contextualized and made accessible to AI agents in a reliable manner. The paper synthesizes current perspectives, highlights challenges around fragmentation and interoperability, and identifies open questions for future research on AI-compatible information management in the built environment.

all_scored.title: ZeroGraph: Compositional Blockwise Training via Materialized Boundary Supervision
all_scored.summary: Blockwise learning can remove online gradient dependencies across depth, but independently optimized blocks need not compose into a useful model. We present ZeroGraph, a systems transformation for pretrained-model conversion and distillation that materializes a frozen teacher's coherent boundary trajectory as a versioned dataset. Each partition then trains with disjoint parameters, optimizer state, random state, and checkpoints, replacing live cross-depth dependencies with persistent supervision. Experiments separate learning quality from systems behavior. On GPT-2 Large, an unanchored objective reduces denoising error by 99.44%, yet assembled held-out cross-entropy worsens from 3.63 to 10.48 and context use becomes negative. A six-arm TinyLlama study identifies clean teacher-boundary regression as the successful interface; the tested noisy objective fails with cached or online targets. The clean recipe passes quality and context-use gates across three Qwen2.5-1.5B seeds and on a 3.086B Qwen2.5 model. In an objective-matched comparison, cached and online targets are bitwise identical. Cached jobs are faster after materialization, but a 618.31 s cache-build cost prevents wall-time break-even through 16 measured reuses. Boundary-shift tests show tolerance to intermediate representation mismatch, and an interrupted block resumes to a bitwise-identical final state without rerunning unaffected blocks. In the tested pretrained-model conversion and distillation setting, cross-depth semantic dependence can move from online optimization into persistent data.

all_scored.title: Conditional Calibration Contracts under Coupled Load: A Branch-Aware Audit of Switched Inference
all_scored.summary: Bursty serving changes both queue states and the population selected for each model. We study conditional calibration contracts as a specification to be validated, rather than a certified property of an existing router. CA-MHD combines load-coupled distillation, closed-loop replay and a cost-informed Schmitt router in a discrete-event simulator with a hardware service table. Across 40 cells (ten training seeds and four content-load coupling levels), we distinguish the original teacher, frozen wide heads on an adapted trunk, and the narrow student. A common teacher-trajectory audit has median absolute student-teacher deficit 0.06 percentage points, but does not certify the student-selected deployment support. Historical results use a kernel correctness gap, not the published SmoothECE; we separately prove selected-branch composition for a residual functional at a common fixed scale. The deployed wide branch has lower ordinal accuracy than the original teacher in all 40 cells. Same-checkpoint student-only serving has lower historical ordinal gap in 27/40 cells; routing also exposes violation tails up to 17.5 percent. Student p99 latency remains above the 1.5 ms target. Retrospective temporal recalibration improves the ordinal gap in 39/40 cells, but causal delayed-label availability is unverified and no incremental per-mode benefit is detected after multiplicity adjustment. An in-sample CUSUM detects 30/40 checkpoint changes at five historical false alarms, with no prospective false-alarm guarantee. These findings support a branch-aware audit and a scoped negative result, not demonstrated routing superiority. Independent budgets, selected-support validation and net utility under a satisfied SLA remain open.

all_scored.title: Reduced Cost Influence Functions for Predict-then-Optimize under Noisy Data
all_scored.summary: Machine learning models deployed in decision-making pipelines, from vehicle routing to dynamic pricing to clinical decision support, must remain reliable in the face of low-quality training data. We study a predict-then-optimize setting in which an upstream model predicts the cost vector of a downstream linear program, with a large pool of noisy training data supplemented by a small curated set of clean data. We introduce Reduced Cost Influence Functions (RCIFs), which combine influence functions from robust statistics with the geometry of linear optimization to estimate how each training point shifts downstream decisions. Building on this, we propose a reweighting algorithm that uses RCIFs to downweight harmful training points and reduce downstream regret. Experiments on random linear programs and shortest-path problems show that our approach reduces regret, and accompanying theory characterizes properties of RCIFs and identifies regimes favorable to our method relative to baselines.

all_scored.title: Back to the Future: Predicting Long-Horizon Dynamics with Retrospective Correction for Disturbance-Aware Retrieval
all_scored.summary: Retrieving objects from densely packed storage requires anticipating how contact disturbs surrounding objects when limited clearance prevents lifting the target over clutter. However, contact can propagate beyond the target's immediate neighbors, while accumulated prediction errors make learned dynamics unreliable over long planning horizons. We introduce DARE (Disturbance-Aware REtrieval), a geometry-aware relational dynamics framework that uses retrospective correction to improve long-horizon prediction for disturbance-aware retrieval. DARE encodes compact object descriptors and predicts action-conditioned disturbance propagation through object-level message passing. When a sparse observation becomes available, a learned corrector uses the prediction discrepancy to amend an earlier predicted state and reruns the intervening dynamics, propagating the correction through the predicted contact chain. These predictions guide a receding-horizon planner that balances retrieval progress against displacement and rotation of surrounding objects, permitting necessary contact while discouraging harmful disturbance. Experiments in planar and RoboCasa environments evaluate long-horizon prediction, generalization, and robustness for disturbance-aware retrieval in dense clutter. See our project website: https://the-back-to-the-future.github.io

all_scored.title: To Align Long, Plan Short: Simulating Diverse Profile-Aligned Students by Realizing Short-Term Plans in Long-Horizon Learning Environments
all_scored.summary: Simulated students offer a scalable way to test learning platforms and AI tutors before deployment with real students and to augment scarce data for studying learning at scale. Existing LLM-based simulators primarily target short, language-centered interactions. In open-ended learning environments, however, student behavior emerges from patterns across long-horizon interaction trajectories, where turn-level prompting can drift from an assigned behavior profile. We introduce ALPS (Align Long-term by Planning Short-term), a hierarchical simulated student conditioned on observable, environment-specific behavior profiles. Rather than selecting every action independently, ALPS alternates between planning profile-aligned task segments and generating the corresponding actions. We evaluate ALPS in both data-sufficient and data-scarce settings, where supervision comes either from real student trajectories or from a teacher LLM. Across both settings, we compare in-context learning (ICL), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward-ranked fine-tuning (RAFT), and their sequential combination (SFT followed by RAFT). Experiments in an inquiry-based physics game and a pharmacy simulation evaluate behavioral density and coverage against held-out real data, and profile consistency using a human-aligned LLM judge. Across both settings, ALPS consistently outperforms turn-level generation, achieving comparable density and judge pass rates under scarce supervision, although coverage remains lower. These results show that hierarchical planning enables faithful, profile-aligned simulation over long interaction horizons, even with limited real student data.

all_scored.title: Watch Your Step: Adam's Margin Maximization Bias Depends on the Learning Rate Schedule
all_scored.summary: We study the implicit bias of Adam and its similarity to sign gradient descent on homogeneous models in binary classification tasks. Perhaps surprisingly, we uncover that these depend on the learning rate schedule. While previous works studied strongly decaying learning rate schedules $η(t)=\mathrm o \left(t^{1/L-1}\right)$, where $L$ is the homogeneity degree, and showed $\ell_\infty$-margin-maximization biases, we focus on the more common complementary regime, including constant and weakly decaying schedules. For a polynomial schedule $t^α$ and homogeneity degree $L$, we show that when $α> \frac 1L - \frac12$, Adam has no trajectory-independent margin-maximization bias for deep linear networks (in the KKT sense): first, there is no non-trivial, locally Lipschitz, convex implicit regularizer in this setting, including any squared norm. Second, on width-$1$ networks, the result holds without requiring convexity, implying that any implicit regularizer for wide networks must be trivial when restricted to a width-$1$ network. Nevertheless, we positively characterize the implicit bias in this regime as maximizing a trajectory-dependent weighted-$\ell_2$ margin for any $L$-homogeneous model. The fundamental mechanism behind our results is convergence of Adam's preconditioner to a trajectory-dependent vector, which also allows showing that the limiting parameter direction depends on initialization. In the intermediate regime $\frac 1L - 1 \leq α\leq \frac1L - \frac12$ we prove an $\ell_\infty$ bias, conditional on gradient directional convergence to a full-support vector. Of independent interest, we establish a loss decay rate for full batch Adam on general homogeneous models, whose leading order depends only on the second-moment parameter.

all_scored.title: Fairness-Aware Design for Contextual Experiments: Guaranteeing Reliability and Equity in Heterogeneous Subgroups
all_scored.summary: Experimental design is critical for evidence-based decision-making in healthcare, marketing, and public policy. However, designing efficient experiments across heterogeneous subgroups presents significant challenges. Existing methods often optimize for statistical power or overall sample efficiency, overlooking crucial fairness considerations across these different subgroups. To address this gap, we introduce a Fairness-Aware Contextual Track-and-Stop Design (F-CTSD) algorithm. The proposed F-CTSD algorithm provides statistical guarantees on subgroup fairness while minimizing required sample sizes. We quantify the fairness-efficiency trade-off and derive the exact sample complexity for the proposed F-CTSD algorithm under its fairness constraints. We further theoretically prove that the proposed F-CTSD algorithm consistently produces accurate treatment effect estimates even under fairness requirements, enhancing statistical reliability. Numerical experiments show that the proposed F-CTSD algorithm outperforms existing methods, achieving higher sample efficiency while reducing subgroup fairness violations by 4.95%.

all_scored.title: The (Butter)fly Dream: Linear Separability of World-Model Rollouts in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model
all_scored.summary: Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly and, on waking, could not tell which was the dream. We ask a version of his question of a model of the fly brain: placed inside a world generated by a world model, can a fixed brain tell that the world is a dream? We treat it as a question about what a connectome-constrained model trained on one task makes available beyond that task: do its responses make the defects of a dream linearly decodable? The observer is a published model of the fly visual system trained only for optic-flow estimation; reality is the MPI-Sintel movie on the model's 721-column retina; dreams are continuations of five real frames by three small world models (a persistence random walk, an MDN-RNN and an RSSM) at three temperatures. The judge is a classifier two-sample test on temporal statistics of cell-type responses, with sequence-level cross-validation. In the trained observer's responses all nine dreams are separable from reality (AUC 0.85-0.99, mean over 50 trained models), in those of the same network before training much less so (0.58-0.75 for the learned world models; paired difference 0.20-0.37), equally on sequences the observer never saw, and in an order unrelated to pixel error. Because these AUCs are near ceiling, we add graded probes made of each window's own real frames with only their order broken. Swapping one adjacent pair of the 14 generated frames gives 0.73 on the trained responses against 0.54 before training and 0.56 for pixel statistics; the trained curve reaches 0.75 at 1.1 swapped pairs of seven, the pixel statistics at 4.7, and the untrained network not at all. A detection horizon, the test on the first k generated frames, orders the world models where the full-length AUC saturates.

all_scored.title: Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair for Safe Vision-Language-Action Models
all_scored.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can generate task-oriented robot actions, but they do not guarantee safe execution in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes. Although CBF-QP safety filters can locally project unsafe actions into a safe set, such correction may push the robot away from the learned task trajectory and leave the VLA policy without a reliable recovery direction. We propose Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair, a post-hoc repair module that uses the short-horizon action chunk predicted by the VLA to detect blocked nominal trajectories and generate entry-exit-rejoin guidance around obstacles. The selected route is added to the CBF-QP objective as a soft guidance term, while the CBF safety constraint remains hard. On SafeLIBERO, our method improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess compared with AEGIS. Our project page is available at GitHub.

all_scored.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions
all_scored.summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.

all_scored.title: Near-Optimal $\sqrt{K}$-Regret for Online Learning in Uninformed Markov Games
all_scored.summary: We study online learning in two-player uninformed Markov games, where the opponent may follow an arbitrary, unknown policy in each episode and the learner does not observe the opponent's actions. [TWYS21] showed that achieving sublinear external regret requires an exponential dependence on the episode length $H$. Motivated by this limitation, they studied the weaker notion of Nash-value regret and obtained an $\widetilde{O}(K^{2/3})$ regret bound, where $K$ is the number of episodes. More recently, [LLZR26] introduced a stronger notion called empirical Nash-value regret and achieved an $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{K})$ bound when the opponent's non-stationarity is moderate, including the case where the opponent follows a fixed policy. However, whether the $\sqrt{K}$ rate is achievable in the worst case remained open. In this paper, we resolve this open question by developing an algorithm that achieves $\widetilde{O}(H^{3/2}S\sqrt{AK})$ empirical Nash-value regret against arbitrary opponent policies, where $S$ is the number of states and $A$ is the number of learner's actions. Specifically, our algorithm combines global and local planning by maintaining a collection of candidate predictions of future losses, each associated with a policy. Global planning learns which candidates to favor across episodes, while local planning combines their policies differently at each state to make decisions. A key ingredient is to coordinate these two components to control the discrepancy between local loss estimates and the total loss of the executed policy, using only the learner's observed trajectories.

all_scored.title: EgoMo3R: Joint Egocentric Motion and Scene Reconstruction
all_scored.summary: Understanding holistic 3D human motion and the surrounding environment from egocentric video is fundamental for applications in AR/VR and robotics. Although these tasks are inherently coupled, existing methods treat them separately. In particular, egocentric motion reconstruction methods typically assume access to metric, gravity-aligned camera trajectories from specialized inertial sensors. Recovering such trajectories from monocular egocentric video remains a significant challenge due to rapid head movements and motion blur. We present EgoMo3R, a joint optimization framework that simultaneously reconstructs 3D human motion and scene geometry from casual egocentric video. It leverages the robustness of low-level visuo-geometric primitives, including monocular depth, optical flow, and point tracks, integrated with a diffusion-based human motion prior via first-order optimization. We propose an alternating optimization scheme that establishes a synergistic feedback loop: scene reconstruction provides physical grounding and trajectory conditioning for the motion prior, while the motion prior regularizes the camera trajectory and anchors the scene in a metric, gravity-aligned world frame. We evaluate EgoMo3R on the highly dynamic sequences of the EgoExo4D and Nymeria datasets and show that it outperforms specialized baselines in both 3D scene reconstruction and egocentric motion estimation.

all_scored.title: Finite-Time Online Sample Complexity for Conditional Diffusion Models
all_scored.summary: We study the finite-time training and sampling error of conditional diffusion models trained by online stochastic-gradient denoising score matching. Rather than assuming access to an exact empirical or population risk minimizer, we analyze the score network produced after a finite number of stochastic-gradient updates under an explicit localized Polyak--Łojasiewicz (PL) condition, stochastic-gradient regularity, and a trajectory-containment assumption. Our analysis separates the network approximation complexity from the online training-sample budget and propagates both errors through the reverse diffusion process. Under anisotropic smoothness, a joint intrinsic-dimensional structure for the data and conditioning variables, sub-exponential tails, and explicit approximation-class compatibility, we obtain a conditional score approximation error of order \[ \widetilde{\mathcal O}\!\left(M^{-η_{\mathrm{app}}}\right), \qquad η_{\mathrm{app}} = \frac{2α_x} {2α_x+d_x'+(α_x/α_y)d_y'}, \] where \(M\) denotes the approximation complexity, \(d_x'\) and \(d_y'\) are the intrinsic response and conditioning dimensions, and \(α_x,α_y\) are their corresponding smoothness exponents. For \(N=RB\) online denoising samples used by SGD, the finite-time optimization error is controlled explicitly in terms of the PL, smoothness, gradient-noise, and initialization constants. Combining these ingredients with reverse-process stability yields a total-variation bound that decomposes into terminal-initialization, time-discretization, approximation/localization, and finite-time optimization errors.

all_scored.title: Adaptive Surface Cleaning under Uncertain Cleaning Response
all_scored.summary: Surface cleaning requires robots to adapt both where they clean and how they interact with contamination whose response to cleaning may vary spatially and remain unobservable prior to interaction. We formulate adaptive surface cleaning as a partially observable Markov decision process and propose a belief-aware planning framework that uses observed cleaning outcomes to update a latent local cleaning-response model and adapt subsequent cleaning motions, forces, and passes. Preliminary grid-world simulations demonstrate the resulting closed-loop planner adapting its spatial decomposition and cleaning actions as the surface evolves.

all_scored.title: Serving Agentic Robot Fleets: Workload Characterization, KV-Cache Thrashing, and Admission Control
all_scored.summary: Agentic robots combine a vision-language brain, a tool-using harness, and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy. Serving a fleet of these agents introduces two coupled resource constraints: the brain repeatedly revisits long, growing key-value (KV) cache states, while the VLA executes action chunks under tight control deadlines. We characterize 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes generated by GPT-6-Astra, RPent, and pi0.5 (1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks), profile both layers on H800 graphics processing units (GPUs), and replay the resulting agent programs on a vLLM serving engine. Brain contexts reach 215k tokens; the median Astra request takes 7.78 s, while the intervening environment-step gap is only 1.0 s. Under a 0.25 s action-chunk deadline, one VLA GPU meets the 1% starvation target for one robot; under a 1.0 s deadline, its measured capacity reaches at least 32. In sustained brain replay, increasing concurrency from 20 to 32 robots reduces throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/s as repetitive prefill displaces generation. A static active-episode cap restores 2.24-2.25 requests/s and raises completed trace-program throughput from 1.30 to 5.00-5.55 episodes/min. Our measurements expose the workload-dependent shift between action deadlines and brain KV residency, and establish practical principles for capacity planning and admission in sustained agentic robot fleets.

all_scored.title: The Verifier Is Part of the Simulator: Evidence-View Gaming in Agentic Equation Discovery
all_scored.summary: A growing number of agentic pipelines search for governing equations: an agent proposes laws and a verifier checks them against simulated trajectories. The verifier sees only a numerical summary: integrals against test functions on a time grid. That summary carries its own discretization error, making the verifier part of the simulator. We freeze the trajectory, candidate library, verifier and thresholds, leaving the agent one move: which permitted summary to admit. Without scores or language models, finer time grids reduce numerical discrepancies and false library rejections. On PDEBench, the verifier instead accepts equations missing diffusion on score-selected summaries. Maximizing a public score rewarding decisive verdicts and larger mismatches when rejecting the library wrongly rejects all 1,500 in-library cases; retrospectively retuning score constants on a separate bank reduces errors to 13/180 at best. We call this evidence-view gaming: reward hacking by choice of permitted summary. In single-turn forced-choice tests, Claude models rarely choose summaries giving wrong verdicts when asked to be accurate, but often do so when asked to maximize the score or report missing physics. In separate trust prompts, they often rank those harmful summaries least trustworthy. Requiring several summaries to agree reduces errors but often withholds a verdict and performs worse than a fixed fine view on PDEBench: a safeguard, not a certificate. Evidence chosen after its verdict is known cannot alone authorize a claim.

all_scored.title: Step-dLLM: Adaptive Step-aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Diffusion LLM Inference
all_scored.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate tokens in parallel via iterative denoising, but their bidirectional attention prevents the KV caching used by autoregressive models and recomputes the full attention map at every step, incurring quadratic per-step cost. Existing sparse attention methods for dLLMs construct a sparse mask after an initial full-attention warm-up and reuse it for the remaining steps, while allocating the sparsity budget uniformly across heads. We argue both choices ignore key structural properties of attention in dLLMs: empirically, attention patterns are only locally consistent across steps and shift abruptly at certain transitions, and different heads concentrate their attention mass to very different extents. To this end, we design Step-dLLM, which periodically refreshes a block-sparse mask at anchor steps along the denoising trajectory and reuses it within each locally consistent interval, while employing a head-adaptive global budget that more aggressively compresses heads with concentrated attention. Backed by a fused IO-aware Triton kernel for block-sparse attention, Step-dLLM applies to pre-trained LLaDA-1.5 and Dream-7B-Instruct without retraining, achieving a 2.78x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention on LLaDA-1.5 at 8K context with 256 denoising steps and 90% sparsity, while improving the accuracy-latency trade-off over prior sparse-attention methods.

all_scored.title: ClothDojo: Learned Data Generation and Benchmarking for Bimanual Garment Flattening and Folding
all_scored.summary: Garment flattening and folding require robots to identify garment structure during manipulation and adapt their actions as the cloth deforms. We present ClothDojo, a simulation platform that generates adaptive manipulation trajectories at scale across diverse garments and initial states and evaluates policies in closed loop. ClothDojo encodes each garment's canonical mesh coordinates as an NOCS texture, providing canonical surface-position cues through the visual interface of a pretrained vision-language-action model. We fine-tune the model on human demonstrations and corrections to obtain a data-generation policy. The policy autonomously generates simulated manipulation trajectories, and we retain rollouts that satisfy task-specific success criteria. Each retained trajectory is re-rendered under a randomly sampled appearance to provide RGB observations for downstream policies that do not receive NOCS. Across both tasks, the policy produces nearly 8,000 successful trajectories over hundreds of garments. RGB policies trained on these generated trajectories outperform those trained directly on the original human demonstrations and corrections across all evaluated garment splits and appearance settings. Evaluations across multiple policy models show that overall performance and appearance robustness vary across models and tasks, while generalization to unseen garments remains a common challenge.

all_scored.title: Lower Bounds on Inference Complexity for Polyak-Ruppert Averaged Stochastic Gradient Descent
all_scored.summary: In this paper, we establish sharp lower bounds for Gaussian approximation of Polyak-Ruppert averaged stochastic gradient descent with polynomially decreasing step sizes. For every fixed exponent $γ\in(1/2,1)$, a single one-dimensional smooth, strongly convex example has approximation error with the limiting variance of order $n^{1/2-γ}+n^{γ-1}$ in Kolmogorov and convex distances. This matches the existing upper bound throughout the range of $γ$. The nonlinear bias contributes $n^{1/2-γ}$ even when the Gaussian reference uses the finite linearized variance. We also derive a lower bound of order $n^{-(1-γ)/2}$ for the relative mean error of estimating the limiting variance from one SGD trajectory, uniformly over a scalar quadratic family. With the limiting variance known, achieving approximation error $\varepsilon$ on this example takes order $\varepsilon^{-4}$ iterations for the best choice $γ=3/4$. Achieving both Gaussian approximation and relative mean variance-estimation errors at most $\varepsilon$ uniformly over the model class requires at least order $\varepsilon^{-6}$ iterations for every fixed $γ$.

all_scored.title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits
all_scored.summary: Mitigating unfair disparities in sequential decision-making is a growing concern in machine learning. We study contextual bandits under a global covariate-based Lipschitz fairness constraint, pioneered by \cite{dwork2012fairness}, requiring individuals with similar contexts to receive similar action distributions. We show that this constraint induces a randomisation region near the decision boundary and explicitly quantify the population level cost of fairness. We further establish a canonical representation of the optimal fair policy, which reduces the fair policy design to a lower-dimensional boundary optimisation problem. We develop a lazy fair greedy algorithm that exploits fairness-induced covariate diversity under continuous contexts, with policy updates computed via finite-dimensional linear programming. For general context distributions, including discrete and mixed contexts, we propose a lazy polyhedral upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm, whose optimistic optimisation reduces to finitely many linear programs over confidence-set vertices. Both methods satisfy fairness at every round and achieve regret of order $O(\sqrt{T} + T^{(d-2)/(d-1)}{\indc\{d\geq 4\}})$ up to poly-logarithmic factors, where $d$ is the dimension of the contexts. A matching minimax lower bound for $\ell_1$-based fairness establishes optimality, and reveals an unavoidable nonparametric cost of learning the decision boundary, which dominates the parametric learning cost when $d \geq 4$. Experiments on synthetic and real data support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.

all_scored.title: Can Jev Improve Demonstration Retrieval for In-Context Learning?
all_scored.summary: Demonstration selection plays a crucial role in the effectiveness of in-context learning (ICL) for large language models (LLMs). Extensive research has explored various retrieval strategies to identify informative demonstrations and improve downstream performance. Recently, the emergence of Jev, a decision-oriented language model capable of producing probabilistic judgments, offers a new perspective on evaluating demonstration utility. This motivates us to investigate a fundamental question: Can Jev improve demonstration retrieval for in-context learning? In this paper, we demonstrate that Jev can effectively enhance demonstration retrieval by directly assessing the utility of candidate demonstrations for a given query. However, applying Jev to large-scale retrieval introduces substantial computational overhead, as each candidate requires an additional decision-making inference. To address this limitation, we propose a simple yet effective knowledge distillation approach that transfers Jev's utility estimation capability to a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP). By learning to approximate Jev's probabilistic judgments, the distilled model enables efficient demonstration ranking while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. Our study highlights the potential of decision-oriented language models for demonstration selection and provides an efficient framework for integrating their decision-making capabilities into ICL.

all_scored.title: Getting a Grip: Operating Human-Agent Software Teams Through Governed Messages
all_scored.summary: Software is increasingly developed by teams in which several people direct many coding agents from different vendors. Such teams must establish who may request what from whom, which messages start work, which decisions bind, and who caused a change.
