all_scored.title: The 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model for Occupational Safety and Health
all_scored.summary: This paper presents the 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model, a progressive framework for Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) management that integrates Job Safety Analysis (JSA), dynamic risk assessment using leading and lagging indicators, and predictive analytics powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). The model provides organizations with a structured pathway to evolve from static, reactive safety practices to a sophisticated, predictive safety paradigm. Each tier builds upon the previous one, creating a comprehensive, data-driven approach that enables just-in-time training and preemptive risk mitigation.

all_scored.title: Multiclass Classification with Rare Useful Features: Fundamental Limits and the Optimality of Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding
all_scored.summary: We consider classification in high-dimensional feature spaces where only a vanishing fraction of features are useful and the number of classes may be large. While this rare-and-weak useful-feature regime is well understood in the binary setting, its multiclass version raises new questions: a feature can be useful for class discrimination without separating any specific pair of classes. We focus on a rare feature diversity model, in which most features are useless, but a small fraction promote discrimination among classes in a way that can be detected by a per-feature diversity test, such as one-way ANOVA or the Kruskal-Wallis test. For this setting, we propose Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding (DP-HCT), a feature-screening procedure that applies a higher-criticism threshold to the collection of p-values obtained from per-feature diversity tests. We justify DP-HCT under a Gaussian multiclass Rare-and-Weak Useful Feature model with class-mean contrasts of fixed magnitude in random directions, extending the binary model of Donoho and Jin (2008). When the number of classes is fixed, our model recovers the binary phase transition. When the number of classes grows logarithmically with the number of features, however, we derive a new and strictly harder phase transition, driven by the growing degrees of freedom and their effect on the useful-feature tail rate. We show that whenever classification beyond chance is possible, DP-HCT with ANOVA, followed by a simple classifier based on similarity to class means, achieves asymptotically perfect accuracy. Experiments on real multiclass classification benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, and numerical simulations confirm that the derived phase-transition curve accurately predicts the finite-sample behavior of DP-HCT in the growing-class regime.

all_scored.title: Partial Invariance for Classification under Structural Causal Models
all_scored.summary: Making predictions in an unseen environment from data collected across multiple training environments is challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced when the target-generating mechanism varies across environments. In this work, we introduce environment-label separation, a form of partial environmental invariance that decomposes the target conditional distribution into an environment-invariant component and a label-invariant component. We show that this partial invariance enables estimation of the target conditional distribution in an unseen environment when using labeled training data together with unlabeled test features. Within the structural causal model framework, we provide sufficient conditions for environment-label separation. Building on these conditions, we develop an algorithm, dIMP-Classifier, which jointly minimizes an estimate of the test risk and encourages invariance across environments. We further provide finite-sample guarantees that characterize the test risk in terms of deviations from invariance, estimation error, and sample complexity. Experiments on simulated data and the real-world light tunnel Causal Chamber data demonstrate that the proposed approach can perform under interventions on the target mechanism and consistently outperforms the considered standard and invariance-based baselines.

all_scored.title: Retrain, Alert, or Rollback? A Three-Response Decision Framework for Production ML Under Concept Drift
all_scored.summary: When a deployed model degrades under concept drift, an operator can retrain it, raise an alert and monitor, or roll back. Yet most drift-adaptation methods consider only retraining. We present RAR (Retrain-Alert-Rollback), a state machine that gives each response an explicit trigger and cost. Retraining is gated on drift detection, label availability, and measured degradation. Every retrained model must pass a two-stage canary before promotion, and corruption-triggered and quality-triggered rollbacks enter different hold states. Under a prospectively specified protocol we compare RAR with six baselines, including a cost-aware retraining policy, on 13 streams: eight real public streams and five semi-synthetic streams derived from them. RAR does not dominate. At low retraining cost, retrain-heavy baselines lead, and no policy's rank differs significantly from RAR's. At higher cost, RAR beats detector-triggered retraining, periodic retraining, and no response simultaneously on four streams, each within a bounded cost window. Its advantage over detector-triggered retraining is consistent with a latency-feasibility condition stated in advance. Against the cost-aware policy, results are heterogeneous. RAR retrains before true drift onsets one eighth to one third as often as detector-triggered retraining, but at lower net utility on most semi-synthetic streams. On H2's designated corruption stream (a registered follow-up), rollbacks fire yet RAR loses to retraining baselines. At $ρ= 1$, removing the canary, and thus rollback, raises utility on 11 of 13 streams. On a post-hoc follow-up stream, cause-specific hold release resumes adaptation where a single cooldown does not. We provide the harness, configurations, and per-cell results for reproduction.

all_scored.title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories
all_scored.summary: AI reviewers are increasingly used to assess scientific manuscripts, yet it remains unclear whether their judgments reflect the improvements authors make through revision. We investigate this question using PaperTrajectory-2026, the 2026 release of PaperTrajectory, a dataset of 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations of changes along 14 dimensions and separate judgments of overall quality. The annotations show that major improvements emphasize empirical evidence and framing, while later revisions tend toward incremental improvement. Using independent assessments of manuscript versions from eight AI reviewers, we examine whether annotated major improvements receive higher scores, which revision dimensions are associated with score changes, and whether user opinions can outweigh observed revision gains. Every reviewer leaves scores unchanged on most major improvements, and agreement on the direction of score changes is weak. Revision dimensions show some reviewer-specific associations with score increases, but provide limited predictive discrimination and no consistent guide across reviewers. Even when a revision earns a higher neutral score, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage, with substantial variation across reviewers. These findings show that substantive revisions are not consistently reflected in review scores and that observed scoring gains can be vulnerable to user framing, motivating assessments that connect manuscript evidence to overall judgments and remain stable when no scientific evidence changes.

all_scored.title: TIGER: Learning from Researcher Taste to Generate Tailored Research Ideas
all_scored.summary: In pairwise comparisons where each judge chooses between an idea generated by its corresponding TIGER-8B policy and one generated by GPT-4.1, the three LLM researchers select the TIGER-8B idea in 56.6%-68.4% of 76 comparisons per researcher. PhD1 and PhD2 select the TIGER-8B idea in 19 of 30 pairs (63.3%) and 17 of 30 pairs (56.7%), respectively. All six directed cross-policy comparisons likewise favor the judge's matched TIGER-8B policy over an off-target policy, supporting the use of individual preference feedback for tailored research ideation.

all_scored.title: Built on Broken Assumptions (BOBA): Why Coding Agents Cannot Be Left Alone
all_scored.summary: Coding agents are autonomous developers. Given a request, they change the code and report back when done. As such, they can handle not only independent requests but whole chains of them, each request built on the last. Agents are known to report wrong work as done, yet benchmarks still test them one request at a time, on human-written code, checked once. We build BOBA-Bench, 280 chains of 20 consecutive requests drawn from 140 real open-source projects, and evaluate ten coding agents on both. All ten do far worse on chains. On average, they complete 95% of requests taken one at a time, but when requests are chained together, they complete 51%. Worse code is not the cause. Once checked, agent code is nearly as good a base for later requests as human code. The cause is the mistakes agents miss. Coding agents declare a request done once their own tests pass, even when those tests miss a mistake. The next request then builds on broken code and fails about twice as often. The mistake is rarely found later. Nor can agents catch such mistakes by reviewing code. Asked whether an implementation is correct, they are right 53% of the time, barely better than a coin flip. Coding agents are therefore heavily dependent on access to verification. A single external ``that's wrong'' after a failed request and one repair round lift chain completion from 51% to 59%, and a repaired mistake no longer hurts the requests that follow. In simpler terms, coding agents are only as reliable as the checks they can reach: without verification, every request that follows is built on broken assumptions.

all_scored.title: Directional Bounded-Confidence Matrix Alignment in Vicsek Flocking
all_scored.summary: This paper proposes a directional bounded-confidence variant of the discrete-time Vicsek multiagent model, in which pairwise heading alignment is modulated by a state-dependent, positive semidefinite matrix that independently gates orthogonal radial and tangential components in the instantaneous line-of-sight frame. We analyze the normalized, matrix-weighted system dynamics, proving a uniform non-vanishing bound on proposal vectors that guarantees global well-posedness across arbitrary network states. For local small-spread states under complete metric interaction, we prove linear geometric contraction of the heading diameter and establish an offline-verifiable spatial bootstrap condition that guarantees metric contact preservation and coincidence avoidance a priori. A counterexample demonstrates invariant polarized states on connected matrix graphs, delineating systemic structural limits. Numerical experiments against unfiltered Vicsek averaging, scalar tied confidence, trace-matched scalar baselines, and restricted-angle rules demonstrate component-selective filtering without rejected-channel leakage, along with improved fixed-bound alignment on multi-seed benchmarks across varying population densities.

all_scored.title: Fuzzy-Enhanced Machine Learning Approach for Type 2 Diabetes Diagnosis
all_scored.summary: Accurate diabetes prediction is critical for early clinical intervention, yet existing machine-learning pipelines often fail due to class imbalance, noisy physiological measurements, and redundant or weakly informative features. To address these unresolved limitations, this study establishes a unified fuzzy-evolutionary-ensemble framework designed to uncover a more discriminative feature space for type 2 diabetes prediction. The workflow integrates selective fuzzification of nonlinear clinical variables, SMOTE-ENN-based balancing and noise filtering, and Bat-Algorithm-driven evolutionary feature selection prior to training a Random Forest classifier. Applied to the Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset, the framework compresses the expanded fuzzy-numerical space into an optimized 10-feature subset and yields substantial performance gains: 96.11% accuracy, 95.14% precision, 98.00% recall, and a 98.23% F1-score. Relative to a baseline Random Forest using all 16 features (74.45% accuracy; 59.86% F1), the system achieves more than a 1.6-fold improvement in F1-score while preserving over 99% stability in majority-class detection and surpassing earlier published 16-feature models impacted by imbalance and weak feature relevance. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the integrated pipeline produces an enhanced fuzzy-numerical representation space that improves diabetes risk stratification and provides a scalable, uncertainty-aware foundation for diagnostic modeling across broader clinical datasets.

all_scored.title: Directional Bounded-Confidence Cucker-Smale Flocking
all_scored.summary: This paper introduces a directional bounded-confidence extension of the Cucker--Smale (CS) flocking model that decomposes pairwise relative velocities into independent radial and tangential channels within the instantaneous line-of-sight frame. Gating these components via compactly supported kernels creates a time-varying, state-dependent, matrix-weighted interaction that strictly generalizes classical scalar CS alignment. We establish an exact energy-dissipation identity with conserved mean velocity and prove exponential velocity consensus under a sliding-window persistent excitation (PE) condition formulated directly on the disagreement subspace. Furthermore, we derive a CS bounded-diameter criterion separating metric decay from aggregate directional coercivity, along with a cluster convergence guarantee. Simulations validate the exact dissipation balance and demonstrate that directional gating successfully restores global alignment in scenarios where traditional isotropic tied-confidence laws remain polarized.

all_scored.title: GoalDex: Learning Image-Goal-Conditioned Policies for Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
all_scored.summary: Dexterous in-hand manipulation is commonly formulated around explicit object pose estimation, yet reliable pose tracking is challenging under severe hand-object occlusions and often requires object-specific supervision. This dependence creates a bottleneck between perception and control that can limit robustness and scalability. We present an end-to-end visuomotor framework for dexterous in-hand reorientation that operates on RGB observations and proprioception without intermediate pose estimation. Our approach jointly learns visual representations and control policies through behavior distillation from privileged state teachers and auxiliary reconstruction objectives. Furthermore, we introduce image-goal-conditioned reorientation, allowing desired object configurations to be specified directly through images rather than canonical pose representations. We evaluate our approach across a diverse set of object geometries and instances in simulation, where it consistently outperforms pose-based methods and policies built on pretrained visual encoders. Finally, we demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer of a single image-goal-conditioned policy across five real-world objects, showing that accurate dexterous reorientation can be achieved without explicit pose estimation. For videos and code release, please refer to the project website: https://rffr.leggedrobotics.com/works/goaldex/

all_scored.title: Restrained Diffusion Bridges: Targeted Denoiser Training and Refinement
all_scored.summary: Diffusion models are often inaccurate in critical, data-sparse regions of the target distribution. Sampling from restrained distributions, biased distributions used in classical enhanced sampling to concentrate data near chosen configurations, can control where training data are collected but biases the learned distribution. We establish that this bias cancels exactly when forward noising from restrained data is conditioned on the restrained configuration at an appropriately chosen intermediate time. This allows a pretrained model fine-tuned on restrained data to achieve high accuracy in any chosen region of the target distribution, regardless of its probability, using standard denoising or flow matching objectives without importance weights. When no target data are available, Gibbs sampling enables inference from a model trained exclusively on restrained data.

all_scored.title: Black-Box Adversarial Example Attacks on Machine Learning based Election Systems
all_scored.summary: Machine learning models have shown exceptional accuracy for ballot classification in election systems. Recent research has demonstrated that these ballot classification models are vulnerable to adversarial example attacks. This is a critical security issue because a successful attack could alter the outcome of an election and undermine the democratic process. However, all adversarial example attacks in the voting domain have assumed a white-box threat model, where the classifier parameters are known. In this work, we advance the field of machine learning in election systems by analyzing a realistic black-box adversary. We implement and evaluate eleven state-of-the-art black-box attacks: query based attacks ADBA, Square, SurFree, RayS, and SA-MOO. We also test adaptive transfer based black-box attacks with APGD-$l_\infty$, APGD-$l_2$, APGD-$l_1$, PGD $l_0$, PGD $l_0$+$l_\infty$, and PGD $l_0$+$σ$. Our attacks span multiple different norms ($l_\infty$, $l_2$, $l_1$, and $l_0$) and three different black-box adversarial threat models (decision based, score based and transfer based). In addition to digital analyses, we physically print and scan $20,000$ adversarial examples to evaluate the real-world performance of different black-box attacks. Our finding demonstrate an even larger physical-digital robustness gap exists for black-box adversarial examples than for white-box adversarial examples. Lastly, we conduct the first ever adversarial example transferability study in the voting domain and test adversarial training and barrier zones as two possible black-box defense strategies.

all_scored.title: Decision Models as Policy Gates for Coding Agents: Explicit Policy Boundaries Improve Detection and Reduce False Alarms
all_scored.summary: Coding agents can destroy data, leak secrets and message the wrong person faster than a human can review. Could a decision model catch these risks at runtime? We evaluated 22 hosted decision models and two prompted general models as classifiers for a multi-rule policy engine. A synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules, with a sealed holdout. With a single shared preamble in both conditions, explicit boundaries written as examples and counterexamples raised recall by 5.5-26.1 percentage points on all 23 available models and reduced false positives on 21. Jev 1.14's recall rose from 89.3% to 98.2%, while unnecessary interruptions fell from 30.6% to 4.8% of 252 clean actions. With examples, its median latency was 120 ms at $0.46 per thousand requests. Strong models retained the recall gains when concrete names were replaced by generic descriptions; three largely retained them when the same boundaries were written as prose. On 16 new scenarios written after the initial studies, a follow-up improved recall on 22 of 23 models and reduced unnecessary interruptions on 21. We release the dataset, rule texts and harness.

all_scored.title: Detailed Derivation of The Backpropagation Algorithm
all_scored.summary: Backpropagation is the standard method for computing the gradients that train neural networks, but it is usually presented in a compact vector form that skips the intermediate steps. This tutorial derives backpropagation step by step for a fully connected feedforward network with sigmoid activations and a squared-error loss. Using a running example with three layers, we first differentiate the error with respect to a single weight by following its path through the network with the chain rule. We then show how summing over all paths leads to the error terms $δ$ and to the four general backpropagation equations in matrix form. Every term is annotated with its dimensions, so each equation can be checked for consistency. The derivation is then extended to $m$ training examples, where the weight gradients become a single matrix product and the bias term corresponds to broadcasting. It is also extended to mini-batch gradient descent, including why the gradient of a mini-batch estimates the full gradient. Batch and mini-batch training are both given as algorithms. Finally, each equation is linked to the corresponding line of a NumPy implementation trained on the AHDBase dataset of handwritten Arabic digits, and the complete code is included.

all_scored.title: When Is Personalized Federated Learning Worth Its Deployment Cost?
all_scored.summary: Personalized federated learning (PFL) may improve client-level performance, but deeper personalization increases deployment cost. We formulate personalization-depth selection as a utility-based empirical decision problem in which client utility equals Macro-F1 minus a cost-sensitivity weight times deployment cost, over six personalization depths labeled P0 through P5. We compare fixed policies with an offline per-client Oracle reference and report allocation maps over Dirichlet data heterogeneity and cost sensitivity. Although evaluated on this hierarchy, the formulation can accommodate any finite candidate set. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a PTB-XL subset, personalization shows empirical, setting-dependent decision regimes rather than a universal benefit: higher cost sensitivity shifts Oracle mass toward the global-only depth P0; low cost sensitivity can favor deeper actions. Patterns are grid observations (three seeds per cell), not theoretical boundaries. Best-uniform is competitive with Oracle assignment (6.5 percent plus or minus 7.8 percent relative regret; 95 percent confidence interval 5.9 to 7.1), whereas random and personalize-all incur much larger regret (189.3 percent plus or minus 367.1 percent and 409.0 percent plus or minus 803.2 percent). Under the same utility, Ditto full-model personalization is substantially suboptimal once cost is counted. The contribution is an offline characterization of when personalization depth is worth its cost, not a new PFL optimizer or deployment-time scheduler.

all_scored.title: History-Aware Force Sensing and Tunable Stiffness in a Pneumatic Kresling Origami Cell
all_scored.summary: Mechanical hysteresis and pneumatic loading complicate contact force estimation from deformation measurements in soft robots. This work presents a 3D-printed polyether block amide (PEBA) Kresling cell with magnetic angular sensing that supports three operating modes: force sensing at zero gauge pressure, force sensing with tunable stiffness under gauge positive pressure, and self-sensing actuation under negative gauge pressure. A multiscale gated recurrent unit (GRU) network estimates contact force from angular histories to account for the the combined effects of geometric deformation and material response. At zero gauge pressure, the model achieves a test RMSE of 0.76~N. Positive gauge pressure approximately doubles the average axial loading stiffness at +20~kPa over the first 3~mm of compression, while pressure-specific models maintain RMSEs below 0.93~N. Under negative gauge pressure, an energy-based compensation model enables contact force estimation using the the model trained at zero gauge pressure, achieving RMSEs of 1.66--2.10~N under quasi-static conditions. These results demonstrate a compact approach to combining force feedback, tunable axial stiffness, and self-sensing actuation in soft origami systems.

all_scored.title: Adversarial Robustness of Retrieval-Based Fact-Checking: Detecting and Mitigating Evidence Contamination
all_scored.summary: Retrieval-based fact-checking systems ground verification in large document collections, creating a critical vulnerability: adversarial evidence contamination. We demonstrate that factually inconsistent but contextually coherent evidence generated to satisfy both retrieval-similarity and linguistic-fluency constraints can systematically mislead verification models. Contaminating just 3.1-7.4% of training corpora with five label-specific strategies causes adversarial content to penetrate up to 35.2% of top-k retrievals, degrading verification accuracy by up to 46.9% relative F1. Existing retrieval-stage defenses, validated against gradient-optimized or syntactically anomalous attacks, transfer poorly to this threat model: detection rates collapse and F1 recovery exhibits high variance across seeds. We propose GLAD (Geometric-Lexical Adversarial Defense), which fuses dense embedding peer-coherence with lexical distributional isolation. Across two benchmarks, two embedding models, and five random seeds, GLAD achieves the highest detection rates (70-86%) and the most consistent F1 recovery, reclaiming 73-80% of contamination-induced degradation on LIAR-RAW while approaching clean baselines on RAWFC. Crucially, unlike defenses that trade clean performance for robustness, GLAD imposes negligible cost on uncontaminated corpora.

all_scored.title: HaloGuard 2.0: An Open-Weights Constitutional Output Guard for Multilingual Response Safety
all_scored.summary: An input guard decides whether a request reaches the model, but never sees what the model says. Harm that emerges during generation, because a jailbreak passed the input layer or a benign request drifted into operational detail, is visible only on the output side and only as tokens arrive. We present HaloGuard 2.0, an open-weight streaming output guard that assigns a safe/unsafe probability to every response token in a single forward pass, so a deployment can stop the stream once harm is confirmed. The guard reuses the constitution of HaloGuard 1.0, our input guard, to organise a 478,532-response training corpus, and supervises each token from the point where the response becomes harmful. We find that a guard trained on conventionally shaped data learns a shortcut specific to streaming: it judges the prompt instead of the response, and handles only 13.9% of matched safe/unsafe response pairs correctly. We correct this with a second phase on 106,043 counterfactual responses built around the base guard's own failure modes, and release the equal-weight average of the base and corrective models. On six English response-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 2.0-0.8B reaches a macro F1 of 83.6 (83.3 on held-out halves of the decision-rule search), up from 72.8, with 38% fewer false positives. It matches the strongest full-response guards with 5-10x fewer parameters and is 2.6 points above the strongest streaming guard, Qwen3Guard-Stream-4B. A multilingual variant, HaloGuard 2.0-Poly-0.8B, trained on PolyGuardMix, reaches 83.1 F1 on the response labels of PolyGuardPrompts across 17 languages, 5.0 points above the strongest baseline. On one H100 the guard costs 0.37 ms per token per stream when moderating 64 concurrent responses. Both guards are hardened continuously through the weekly red-teaming protocol of HaloGuard 1.0, extended here to the output layer.

all_scored.title: Semantic Interoperability in Federated Digital Twin Systems: A Systematic Review Through the Levels of Conceptual Interoperability Model
all_scored.summary: When two companies connect their digital twins, software models of their plants kept up to date with live data, each twin must translate the other's data into its own terms, and that translation rule, called a mapping, can stop being correct when one company changes the meaning of its data without telling the other. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review screened 5,833 records and read 119 full texts to determine whether any published system detects such a broken mapping and repairs it while the twins operate. In all 32 included studies the mapping is fixed before operation, and the two ingredients of run-time repair appear only separately: cross-company matching without any check that the match still holds, and detection and repair of changed meaning within a single company. The review turns this gap into six requirements, each illustrated on one running example, that a system claiming run-time semantic interoperability between independently owned twins should meet.

all_scored.title: Bounded Retained History in a Proxy Flow Replay: A Mixed Predictive Pilot and an Allocation Study
all_scored.summary: We examine bounded retained history through a frozen predictive pilot and a subsequent allocation study on a curated UNSW-NB15 flow mirror. Both use an artificial release-order replay based on raw ltime ticks, with equal-tick records querying a shared prior-group state. In the pilot, the model with added retained relational features had lower reconnaissance recall than the current-flow-plus-counters baseline (43.66% versus 47.84%) and lower benign false-positive rate (3.63% versus 6.68%) at separately frozen operating thresholds, together with lower AUROC. This mixed result did not establish a predictive advantage. A development-only audit subsequently found that capacity eviction dominated expiration in the 256-record, 300-tick FIFO state, with a median completed record lifetime of 11 ticks. A protocol specified before its single execution, but after the pilot and post-hoc mechanism audit, compared five label-blind retention arms on the already-used development trace. Its primary equal-source endpoint averaged retained/reference ratios for service-expanded source out-degree and source-destination service diversity. Source-balanced retention at 256 records exceeded FIFO-256 by a pooled endpoint difference of 0.440738 and met the prespecified materiality and subblock rule. Crucially, the event-weighted ratios for both quantities decreased relative to FIFO-256: the result is specific to the equal-source weighting objective and does not establish uniformly improved retention. The study supplies neither evidence of detection improvement nor an explanation of the pilot result. Reused data, concentrated reconnaissance support, proxy timing, and the absence of a qualified independent corpus bound the interpretation.

all_scored.title: Testing concept-level audits of melanoma classifiers with diffusion counterfactuals and matched positive controls
all_scored.summary: Concept-based explanations of melanoma classifiers are rarely tested against controls with known targets. We built a counterfactual audit from a diffusion model conditioned on seven 7-point checklist concepts and tested it with such controls. Colour-calibrated start noise reduced colour outliers from 78.5-84.8\% to 6.6-13.3\%. Four of seven knobs were target-dominant but also changed other concepts. Quartile-based positive controls were confounded, and the audit failed its pre-specified rule. It recovered the targets of all 16 controls matched on the generator's pseudo-labels and of 12 of 12 controls labelled by a second evaluator, for three concepts; concept activation vectors recovered fewer (11 of 16). In 18 permuted-label classifiers, significant sweep responses and target rankings also arose, whereas standardised effect margins separated the controls from these null classifiers. The pigmentation sweep raised the melanoma logit in 15 of 15 ISIC 2020 classifiers (+3.12 on average) and 6 of 6 HAM10000 classifiers (+4.01), about four times the null response in scale-free units; the regression effect did not transfer. An exploratory decomposition, evaluated against the controls, suggested that knob cross-talk partly hides vascular responses. Matched controls and null classifiers are practical checks of concept audits.

all_scored.title: Order-Only On-Policy Distillation
all_scored.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generations by matching the teacher's token probabilities. These probabilities entangle two kinds of information: which tokens the teacher prefers, and how confident it is. The latter reflects the teacher's own capacity and calibration, which a smaller student may be unable to reproduce. Because the teacher temperature changes these values without changing the ordering, OPD is also sensitive to the temperature choice. We ask whether the teacher's ordering of candidate tokens is enough, and propose Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O$^{3}$PD). At each student-generated prefix, O$^{3}$PD trains the student to reproduce the order of the teacher's top-$K$ tokens, without fitting their probability values. The objective is therefore invariant to the teacher temperature and needs no temperature tuning. Across six teacher--student pairs, O$^{3}$PD outperforms OPD on the average over HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25 in every pair, by up to 2.9 points, with gains of up to 5.6 points on AIME25. Other ranking losses yield similar gains, so the benefit comes from ordinal supervision itself. Analysis shows that O$^{3}$PD departs further from the teacher's probabilities than OPD, yet reproduces its ranking more faithfully and yields a stronger student. The ranking, not the probability values, thus carries the knowledge that on-policy distillation needs to transfer.

all_scored.title: ZT-DAC: ML-Driven Dynamic Access Control Policy for Zero Trust in DER Networks
all_scored.summary: The increasing penetration of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) in the smart grid has significantly expanded the cyber-attack surface. Traditionally, DER networks rely on static role-based access control (RBAC) mechanisms that assume persistent trust after authentication. This limitation enables adversaries to maintain unauthorized privileges and move laterally across DER systems, disrupting grid operations. Although attribute-based access control (ABAC) enables fine-grained and context-aware access decisions, it does not fully eliminate implicit trust. Zero Trust (ZT) principles can be incorporated to enhance ABAC policies. This paper proposes a dynamic access control framework for implementing ZT in DER networks (ZT-DAC). The proposed solution employs a two-stage verification process and integrates an Open Policy Agent (OPA)-based RBAC with a machine learning (ML)-based ABAC to enforce continuous and adaptive trust score assessment. To support realistic DER operations, a DER-specific access control model is developed and used to generate a domain-informed dataset of access requests incorporating both legitimate and adversarial behaviors. Experimental results on the dataset show that the OPA-based decision layer achieves \(91.92\%\) accuracy, with a False Positive Rate of \(14.45\%\), while the ML model achieves a Mean Absolute Error of \(2.074\) and an \(R^2\) of \(0.891\) in trust-score prediction. The ABAC layer achieves \(93.27\%\) accuracy, with a FPR of \(3.88\%\), validating its practical feasibility within realistic DER environments.

all_scored.title: When Delay Meets Drift: Physical Safety of Robot Foundation Models Is a Cross-Layer Problem
all_scored.summary: Robot foundation models now act in a closed loop, yet their safety is evaluated one variation at a time: robustness benchmarks perturb the scene while assuming instantaneous inference, and real-time execution methods study inference delay in nominal scenes. We argue that physical safety is not a property of the model alone, but emerges from how variations in the physical environment, the model, the computing platform, and execution interact in closed loop. We formalize this as cross-layer variation propagation across these system layers and use an interaction contrast to measure when joint variation creates more risk than the sum of its parts. In 4,000 paired closed-loop episodes of the pi0.5 vision-language-action model on LIBERO, a 400 ms inference delay raises the safety-violation rate by 3.5 percentage points under the training viewpoint but by 37 percentage points under a 60-degree camera shift: 33.5 percentage points (95% CI: 25-43) more than the two effects combined. We close with a research agenda toward predictable physical intelligence: predicting when variation becomes risk, and adapting compute, power, and control accordingly.

all_scored.title: EarthJev: Calibrated, Non-Generative Answers to Natural-Language Questions about Sentinel-2 Land Cover
all_scored.summary: Vision-language models for remote sensing answer questions about satellite images by generating text: every answer costs a decoding loop, has to be parsed back to an option, and comes without a usable probability. We present EarthJev, a 0.8B-parameter model that answers typed questions about multispectral Sentinel-2 patches without generating any token. All 12 bands enter the vision encoder of Qwen3.5-0.8B through a widened input layer initialised from the RGB kernels, and, following the open OneJev recipe, the answer is read from the logits of the option letters at a single position and trained with cross-entropy plus Brier score. Under a pre-specified analysis plan, we compare it with the same backbone fine-tuned to generate the answer and with three multimodal language models fine-tuned with LoRA, all trained on the same 70,890 questions from 5% of BigEarthNet v2.0 and timed in one job on the same GPU; VQA models that classify over a fixed answer vocabulary are reported as a reference for the cost of answering only the questions seen in training. EarthJev answers a question in 19.9 ms, 4.3 to 8.7 times faster than the multimodal language models and 6.8 times faster than its own backbone used generatively; when all the questions about an image are asked together, it answers them in 42.8 ms, 3.7 to 10.1 times faster than the batched generative models. On 36,028 test questions it reaches 86.0% accuracy (three seeds), 0.6 and 1.2 points below the two 2B multimodal models and 3.5 points below the remote-sensing EarthDial-4B, with answers that are valid by construction and calibrated probabilities (ECE 0.006). Replacing the nine non-RGB bands with their mean costs 4.5 points, so the model uses the multispectral input, and in an ablation training the whole vision encoder raises accuracy to 88.4% at the same cost. Code and model: https://github.com/CosmoIknosLab/EarthJev

all_scored.title: HQNN-CL: Regime-Aware Hybrid Quantum Neural Network with Continual Learning for Financial Forecasting
all_scored.summary: Financial time-series forecasting is still difficult owing to the non-stationary nature of the market, regime changes, and catastrophic forgetting, which makes conventional deep learning models hard to adapt in the long term. To achieve uncertainty-aware robust financial forecasting in the face of changing market conditions, this study proposes a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Network with Continual Learning (HQNN-CL). The proposed framework combines Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) based regime detection, BiLSTM temporal encoding, adaptive-depth parameterized quantum circuits, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), experience replay, and probabilistic forecasting in a single architecture. The framework was tested on four real-time stock datasets: Microsoft, Systems Limited, Teradata and Tata Consultancy Services, and compared with seven state-of-the-art forecasting models, including recurrent and Transformer-based models. The experimental results show that HQNN-CL has outperformed other methods on the Systems Limited (RMSE = 3.0149) and Teradata (RMSE = 0.8909) datasets and is within 0.32% and 0.40% of the best baseline method for Microsoft and Tata Consultancy Services, respectively. The proposed framework also generates well-calibrated probabilistic forecasts within the range of 89.5% to 96.5% empirical coverage rate, has zero catastrophic forgetting (BWT = 0.0000) for all sequential learning tasks, and consistently shows positive forward transfer. Ablation and statistical significance analyses also validate the performance of adaptive quantum feature learning and continual adaptation under heterogeneous market conditions, regime-wise.

all_scored.title: State-Aware Virtual Patient Simulation for Training Psychiatrists in Challenging Clinical Scenarios
all_scored.summary: Psychiatrists must be prepared to manage patients exhibiting challenging psychological states, including suicidal ideation, hallucinations, and other high-risk behaviors. However, opportunities to safely practice such interactions are limited. While recent conversational agents can simulate patients, existing approaches largely rely on large language models (LLMs) to determine patient responses, making it difficult to consistently maintain psychological state, adapt to the clinician's responses, and generate clinically plausible challenges that meaningfully test the clinician. We present a state-aware virtual patient simulation pipeline for training psychiatrists in challenging clinical scenarios. The proposed system maintains an evolving patient state throughout the interaction and orchestrates patient behavior rather than leaving response generation entirely to an LLM. At each interaction, a learning-based behavioral strategy selector determines the type and level of challenge appropriate to the current patient and clinician context. The selected strategy, patient state, clinician response, interaction history, and relevant clinical knowledge are then provided as grounded context to an LLM to generate a semantically relevant and psychologically consistent patient response. Following each session, the system analyzes the interaction and provides feedback to the clinician on their communication and management of the virtual patient.

all_scored.title: Large Geometry Models Are Priors For Fast Physics Pretraining
all_scored.summary: Language and vision models became data-efficient by pretraining on plentiful unlabelled data; physical field models have such data, over ten million 3D shapes, but geometry pretraining designs its targets rather than deriving them from the physics. Euler-Lagrange geometry pretraining derives them: for attached flow, a shape enters the flow's Euler-Lagrange equation only through coefficients that distance and normal line (the normal up to sign) fix to first order. Their reconstruction error therefore bounds what a representation loses about any field, and fine-tuning on costly simulations need only assemble the global field. We realise it in AREALS, a masked surface autoencoder whose areal tokens carry position, normal and area, pretrained self-supervised and sign-free on 61,822 raw meshes. Because the operating condition enters only through the far field, sensors can supply it: AREALS completes a hidden field in one forward pass without condition labels. It matches the accuracy of the same architecture trained from scratch with half the simulations on DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++ and about a quarter on WindsorML. On DoubleDelta wings, 20 sensors give $3.9\times$ and $4.0\times$ lower field and force error than GABI, a Bayesian inversion method with a learned prior, and beyond the training angles pretraining halves the error.

all_scored.title: Fragility Is Not Reducible to Hardness: Conditional Causal Difficulty for LLMs
all_scored.summary: Large language models show large and seemingly arbitrary performance drops when a task is rewritten in ways that leave its requirements untouched. We recast task difficulty as a causal quantity: the treatment effect of meaning-preserving perturbations on a model. A meaning-preserving rewrite can only be observed to hurt a task the model can already solve, so we place the estimand on the principal stratum where the degradation occurs: the conditional causal difficulty (CCD), the probability that a randomly drawn twin breaks a solvable task. Because harder tasks tend to be more phrasing-sensitive, complexity enters as an effect modifier rather than a confounder, and we residualize it out to obtain complexity-residualized difficulty (CRD); zero for a task exactly as fragile as its complexity predicts, positive for anomalously fragile ones. Current benchmarks do not supply the data CCD requires, so we introduce GlassGSM and GlassMATH, augmenting GSM8K and MATH with twins built from perturbation families, raising fragility on GlassGSM by $\approx 12\times$ over GSM-IC-style distractors on the same problems ($3.7\%\to44.9\%$) while keeping the answer key unchanged. Our predictor Frail learns the per-perturbation break probability and reaches $0.613{\pm}0.023$ of the suite reliability ceiling on GlassGSM and $0.557{\pm}0.023$ on GlassMATH, against $0.171$/$0.401$ for a surface-feature baseline and $0.444$/$0.463$ for supervised baselines such as VAP3, and, at a $5\%$ curation budget on GlassGSM, doubles random recall of fragile items, matching an oracle ranking. Additionally, cross-fitted residualization leaves CRD uncorrelated with the declared proxy in practice. Code is available at https://github.com/upwork/Conditional_Causal_Difficulty_for_LLMs

all_scored.title: Same Function, Different Gradients: Evaluating Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization
all_scored.summary: Gradients are no longer used only to train models: Gradient magnitudes are now measurement instruments, used to rank attention heads for pruning, to decide per-example clipping in private training, to allocate adapter rank budgets, and to debug models. Across these workflows, larger gradient magnitudes are taken to mean greater importance. Even for a fixed input--output function, these gradients are computed in one of many possible parameter coordinate systems. For example, attention scores depend on the query and key projections only through the paired product $W_QW_K^\top$. Scaling a head's query projection by $c$ and the corresponding key projection by $1/c$ therefore leaves every output logit unchanged. This change in parameter coordinates rescales the corresponding query and key gradient norms by $1/c$ and $c$, respectively. To test whether gradient-based decisions remain unchanged under these coordinate changes, we introduce Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization (GRR). GRR rewrites a trained model in new parameter coordinates that compute exactly the same function, verifies that predictions are unchanged, and then tests whether the decisions derived from the gradients are unchanged too. Our audits span GLUE classifiers, a ViT on CIFAR-10, GPT-2-medium and GPT-2-large, a 1.1B-parameter Llama-style model on WikiText-2, and six trained LoRA adapters. Empirically, predictions are preserved throughout, but both the gradients and the gradient-based decisions change. Across 66 GLUE attention audits, the median top-3 overlap of raw head-gradient rankings is only $1/3$, and rankings and pruning masks change even under the mildest rescalings we test. In the largest of 14 global-pruning audits, the shifted ranking selects head masks that differ in four of 22 pruned heads and reach $50.92\%$ and $94.84\%$ validation accuracy on one ELECTRA SST-2 model.

all_scored.title: Beliefs in feedback: Factored representations of interacting agents in transformers
all_scored.summary: Complex systems, from ecosystems to brains, are usually modeled as modular components coupled through feedback rather than as indivisible wholes. Can a transformer trained on the joint behavior of a group of interacting agents be understood in the same way? In this work, we develop a computational-mechanics framework to study agents interacting in feedback loops. We formally prove that any joint stochastic process can be presented as resulting from the behavior of agents interacting in feedback, and the resulting process is generated by a hidden Markov model whose Bayesian beliefs factorize into separate components per agent. Furthermore, our experiments show that transformers trained on such feedback sequences make use of this separability, disentangling the beliefs about the underlying factors into separate subspaces of their residual stream. This representation is found to scale linearly (instead of exponentially) with the number of agents. Moreover, interventions show that these representations are causally efficacious, allowing for targeted steering of individual agents' beliefs by selectively inserting counterfactuals. However, coarse-graining the behavior is found to disrupt the factorization, and can force a higher-dimensional representation. Together, the results establish both the dimensional advantage of a factorized representation and the ability of transformers to exploit it, laying the groundwork for investigating traces of compositional predictive architecture in pretrained models.

all_scored.title: METER: Matched-Event Calibration for Short-Event EEG Microstate Transition Analysis
all_scored.summary: Short cognitive events contain unequal and often sparse transition evidence, so raw EEG microstate distances can reflect finite sampling rather than neural reconfiguration. We introduce METER (Matched-Event Transition Estimation against a Reference), a participant-relative framework that separates marginal occupancy from conditional next-state choice and evaluates each event against duration-conditioned events from a fixed participant-specific reference bank. METER-Jump integrates uncertainty in sparse target and reference transition tables, returning a randomized event rank for testing and a continuous standardized coordinate for association analysis. Using a reproducible three-state representation selected by spatial criteria, we evaluated METER with participant-fitted simulations, estimator ablations, map perturbations, and preprocessing sensitivities. Event-level false-positive rates were 0.044-0.056 across four heterogeneous null mechanisms. By contrast, global cutoffs learned under the participant-fitted null and transferred unchanged to other regimes produced false-positive rates from 0.004 under rare transitions to 0.234 under map perturbation; duration-conditioned ranks remained near 0.05. Detection probability was approximately 0.69 with fixed maps but fell to 0.22 after bootstrap-derived map-assignment perturbation. In 4,175 natural-reading events from 18 participants, no linguistic association survived multiplicity correction in the primary 30-ms analysis, although a 20-ms sensitivity changed one within-stream max-$T$ decision. METER therefore calibrates finite-event departures conditional on a defined microstate sequence, while map assignment, filtering, temporal smoothing, and reference construction remain separate sources of measurement uncertainty.

all_scored.title: ECGJev: Question-Conditioned Option Scoring for 12-Lead ECG Interpretation
all_scored.summary: Clinical interpretation of a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) often requires answering targeted diagnostic questions with clear, quantifiable decisions. We introduce ECGJev, the first ECG framework built on a decision decoder, a pretrained language model trained to return a probability for every listed option. A question-conditioned bridge compresses frozen waveform and spectrogram features into 16 ECG tokens, and a two-stage procedure adapts the bridge and low-rank adapters on the decoder's native option readout using diagnostic labels alone, scoring all options for a question in one forward pass. Evaluated across four ECG benchmarks, ECGJev achieves the highest macro-F1 on CPSC2018 (80.46%), PTB-XL (71.68%) and Chapman (96.86%), and generalizes competitively to the small-sample PTB cohort. Concept probes and perturbation analyses further show that its predictions rely directly on the ECG input, remain stable under option-order and wording variations, and transfer zero-shot to unseen waveform concepts. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhuoyuanli-lab/ECGJev.

all_scored.title: SensOFormer: Foundation Models for Particle Accelerators
all_scored.summary: Large-scale scientific facilities, such as particle accelerators, are complex systems composed of thousands of interacting components that must operate collectively to support diagnostics and control, and ensure safe, reliable operation. These facilities rely on extensive sensor networks that generate large volumes of heterogeneous, incomplete, and noisy telemetry, often sampled at different rates across subsystems. In this paper, we adopt the foundation-model paradigm to learn general-purpose sensor representations from historical accelerator data through self-supervised pretraining. We introduce SensOFormer, a denoising masked transformer with a Perceiver-style encoder-decoder architecture designed to handle variable sensor sets, accommodate heterogeneous sampling rates, and learn robust representations from noisy measurements. The model is pretrained on multiple particle-accelerator datasets and transferred to downstream tasks, including missing-data imputation, anomaly detection, cavity identification, and fault identification. Through extensive evaluations and comparisons, we demonstrate that a single self-supervised model can learn reusable representations for diverse operational tasks in large-scale scientific facilities. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/sensoformer.

all_scored.title: Query-efficient scan-and-search watermark localization
all_scored.summary: Recently, the detection of AI-generated content has been of particular importance in various fields of our society. For accountability purposes, many large language models (LLMs) have implicitly watermarked their outputs. Localizing such watermarks requires a piece of text to undergo an additional verification process. Existing localization methods typically rely on dense token-level scoring, making verification costly even when an LLM-generated watermark only sparsely appears. To tackle this problem, we design a new adaptive allocation strategy that first maintains broad document coverage and then progressively concentrates the detection budget on regions that exhibit stronger watermark evidence or are more likely to contain watermarked content. We then transform the statistical signals from the selected regions into e-values and employ the proposed token-weighted e-BH procedure to determine the localized watermark regions. The resulting framework is called BELL (Budgeted E-evidence Localization for LLM Watermarks). Theoretically, BELL can control the token-weighted false discovery rate (FDR) without independence assumptions across regions. Finally, extensive experimental results demonstrate that BELL consistently outperforms competing methods across multiple LLMs, datasets, and watermarking schemes.

all_scored.title: Uncertainty-Aware 3D Position Reconstruction in CZT Drift-Strip Detectors
all_scored.summary: Accurate three-dimensional interaction-position reconstruction is important for CZT drift-strip detectors, but conventional methods can suffer from degraded performance in challenging detector regions, while learned models provide limited information about prediction reliability. We investigate two uncertainty-aware approaches: deep ensembles of point-estimation networks and simulation-based inference (SBI), which estimates a posterior distribution over interaction position. Both approaches are trained on physics-based simulations and evaluated on both synthetic and experimental data. On synthetic data, uncertainty from both methods correlates with positioning error, with SBI showing a substantially stronger relationship. On experimental measurements, the deep ensemble achieves improved $z$-position resolution, while SBI provides more informative uncertainty estimates that highlight regions of reduced positional information and discrepancies between simulation and the physical detector. These results demonstrate the complementary strengths of ensemble-based reconstruction and posterior inference for uncertainty-aware detector position reconstruction.

all_scored.title: Scaling Makes It Possible: How Large Models Master Impossible Languages
all_scored.summary: While language models (LMs) excel in natural language tasks, their ability to learn impossible languages--those that violate the structural, cognitive, or logical constraints that make human languages learnable and functional--remains debatable. This controversy is further fueled by a divide between linguistic theorists and empirical researchers working with small-scale LMs. To address this controversy, we introduce semantic coherence. This concept measures how effectively semantic information is expressed in language structures and examines the learning capabilities of LMs across multiple scales. By fine-tuning billion-parameter LMs on impossible language samples, we demonstrate that larger LMs achieve similar performance on impossible and possible languages, whereas million-parameter LMs exhibit significant degradation when trained on impossible languages. This performance gap widens as semantic complexity increases. We further show that scaling up the LM size fundamentally shifts the learning focus from grammatical rules to semantic understanding, with billion-scale LMs exhibiting a threefold reduction in sensitivity to low-level linguistic perturbations while maintaining stable performance under high-level semantic perturbations.

all_scored.title: MIRA: Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation
all_scored.summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a deployed model using only unlabeled target data, but standard entropy-based methods often rely on deterministic confidence and can reinforce overconfident errors under distribution shift. We propose MIRA, Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation, a source-free online adaptation method that uses lightweight last-layer Gaussian perturbations to probe prediction reliability. For each target batch, MIRA reuses a single feature extraction pass and samples perturbed classifiers around the source classifier, forming an efficient local predictive distribution. Rather than fitting a Bayesian posterior, MIRA treats the perturbation scale as a local probing radius and selects a batch-specific scale using mutual information (MI) and prediction agreement. The resulting perturbation-sensitivity signal identifies predictions that are confident and locally stable under classifier perturbations, while suppressing brittle predictions with high stochastic disagreement. MIRA then performs adaptation with an MI-confidence weighted entropy loss, which down-weights perturbation-sensitive or low-confidence samples before they drive entropy minimization. This weighted loss reduces the influence of brittle predictions that can otherwise cause harmful adaptation under distribution shift. The method requires no source data, retraining, model ensembles, or offline posterior fitting, and can be applied as a plug-and-play modification to entropy-minimization TTA. Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks show improvements in accuracy, calibration, and negative log-likelihood, suggesting that mutual-information-guided perturbation probing and weighted adaptation yield more robust online TTA than deterministic confidence.

all_scored.title: Safety4DM: A Vision-Language Framework for Risk-Aware Dynamic Maps in Vehicle-Road-Cloud Collaborative Driving
all_scored.summary: Dynamic map (DM) is a core information infrastructure for vehicle-road-cloud (VRC) cooperative autonomous driving. It fuses perception data from multiple sources to overcome the inherent line-of-sight and field-of-view limits of single-vehicle perception. However, DM still falls short on driving safety in two ways. First, DM data specifications already define road conditions semantically, but no pipeline yet turns real-world road observations into fine-grained risk entities in the DM. Second, existing DM systems lack a natural language interface for driving risks. To close these gaps, we propose Safety4DM, a safety-oriented language system for VRC dynamic maps. We first build RoadRisk, a real-world road image dataset that covers four types of road conditions and four risk levels. On this dataset, we fine-tune a vision-language model (VLM) for road safety risk perception. The model outputs structured risk representations that the DM can ingest directly. We then introduce a Safety-aware Step-wise Prompting (SafeStep) mechanism as the natural language query interface of the DM. SafeStep answers queries accurately and also generates actionable driving advice. To build and evaluate this interface, we develop SafeVRC-Sim, a VRC cooperative simulation framework, and SafeDM-QA, a safety question-answering benchmark. Experiments show that even the compact Qwen3-VL-4B reaches 89.83% accuracy on risk perception after fine-tuning. SafeStep also plugs easily into multiple LLM families. With medium and large models (20B and above) from five families, it achieves over 93% natural language query accuracy in every case, which shows strong generalization.
